speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (acting Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
As I understand, the
road from Edmunston to Moncton is completed and has been under operation for a year and a half. The other part of the road, from Quebec east, the contractors expect to have completed and ready to hand over to the commission about the 1st of August, and after that it will be ready for operation through from Quebec to Moncton.
Have any arrangements been made for the operation of the road between Quebec and Moncton when it is completed?

No- arrangement has been
made for the operation. That would not be taken up until the road was ready to be handed over.

That would seem to be a very poor policy on the part of my hon. friend. He will have a hiatus, I am afraid, in the operation. There seems to be a great demand that that road should be operated.
I am speaking now largely from the standpoint of the people of the province of New Brunswick. We have thought for a long while that it would be a great advantage if that road were opened up in order to afford arother outlet for lumber and agricultural products, and I would think that the minister would get busy and have an arrangement made before the railway is actually completed so that when it is handed over a train service could be operated over it. I think we should have some announcement from the minister as to what will be done.

As the hon. member knows, that part between Moncton and Edmunston has been operated for the last year and a half. During the last year, and until a few days ago, that part from Quebec to a station called Monk was operated by the Quebec Central railway. When the road is corn-281	KEVISED
pleted the Grand Trunk Pacific will have the first right to take it over and operate it if they so desire. But if they do not wish to take over this portion arrangements will be made that the road will be operated between Quebec and Moncton until the Grand Trunk Pacific are prepared to take the whole line over. Arrangements will have to be made with the Grand Trunk Pacific to take over a portion of the road on certain conditions. If they do not wish to take over that portion there will be no trouble about the operation of the road, either by the Intercolonial railway or by some arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific until the whole road is completed.

I feel that the Government have not accomplished what might have been accomplished in the way they have managed this road in the past year and a half. I am not saying this in a faultfinding spirit; I am only pointing out to the minister wherein he has failed to make its operation of benefit to the public and to the road itself. I complained a year ago about the hard and fast rules by which the road seemed to be bound in regard to freight rates. The difficulty seems to be that it is being run as a purely local proposition. If a man has lumber to ship to Boston-and usually all lumber produced along the line of the road goes to the American market-the road will not give* a through rate and take their proportions of that rate. The only thing they will do is take a local rate from point to point that will be three or four times as great as the proportions for that distance on a through rate. I had a case of my own which, I pointed out to the Hon. Mr. Cochrane, where I was charged six cents a hundred pounds for hauling lumber some twenty-three or twenty-five miles. I could get that lumber transported to Boston, 500 miles, for about 13 cents; but I was asked to -pay a local rate of 6 cents. The result was that I did not ship the lumber over the Transcontinental. I was able to haul it fifteen miles over toad roads and ship it by the Canadian Pacific railway. Last year they cut the rate down to 4 cents, and we then shipped our lumber over the road. I think probably we saved a little by doing so. It always has struck me that while it is -admitted tfhat there must be a slightly higher charge in proportion for a short haul than for a long haul, a charge of 4 cents for twenty-three or twenty-five miles is entirely out of proportion to a 13 cent rate for nearly 500 miles. If the management would quote

a through rate from any point on the road to Boston and charge us only a reasonable proportion of it, I am satisfied that a greater amount of business could be developed. I also think that daily passenger trains each way would pay. My experience in public utilities has been that the better the service you give the public the more business you obtain. Give people the opportunity to patronize your utility and they will patronize it. rue present arrangement is very unsatisfactory. The train leaves Moncton in t..e morning, runs to Edmunston and returns the next day. That is a pretty slow method of transportation. The result is that the Canadian Pacific railway get practically all the business. If a better service were given, with better freight rates, 'I believe the minister could prob-
4 p.m. ably make more money. In saying this I believe I am voicing the sentiments of the business people of that district.

The service, of course, could hardly be expected to be satisfactory with a train going up one day and down the next. I agree that through rates should be given; but the Grand Trunk Pacific refuse to take the road over and temporary arrangements were made with the Intercolonial railway to operate to Edmunston. While it has been operated by the Intercolonial railway, there has been a serious loss every month, and the rates probably have been a little high for that reason. Now that the road is practically completed, or within a couple of months of being completed, trains will be running through from Quebec to Moncton and I think the grievances that the public must have had in the way of inadequate train service and high freight rates will be overcome. I understand that the Intercolonial railway have made arrangements to take out some four million feet of lumber from that road, a lumber which has been there for a couple of years. An arrangement has been made to move that lumber.
From what point?

Some place near Edmundeton. I forget the name of the people who are moving out the lumber but they are doing everything to satisfy the people along the line. As I have said, the road will be finished in a couple of months and the Intercolonial or the Grand Trunk Pacific will operate it through to Quebec.
What arrangements were made with the Quebec Central?

The arrangement was made last fall. Of course, the contractors could not go on with the work in the winter months and so an arrangement was made with the Quebec Central to operate the road during that time. The contractors were to resume wrork on the first of May, but I think the time has been extended', to the 15t,h of May. Within a couple of months at the most the road will be completed and handed over to the commission.

I think that the section of the road that the Quebec Central are' operating is about completed now. I saw the general manager of that road a short time ago and he told me that they were able to draw out a train of sixty-six loaded cars with the little engines they use on the Quebec Central, but when they get the train on their own road they 'have to break it up into three or four sections. It would seem therefore, that that section of the road is in pretty good shape. I am one of those who have some material along: that line which I would like to have hauled out, but the Quebec Central are charging from four to six and seven cents a hundred to haul the stuff out over the Grand Trunk Pacific, and then there is the through rate, in addition. Lumber and pulpwood is a class of freight that cannot stand high rates and when four cents to six cents a hundred is added it takes away all the profit and a little more. Inasmuch as this road is completed for over 100 miles I should think the Government could arrange for the Grand Trunk Pacific to take over and operate it as part of their new system and to give us through rates. A large amount of lumber is waiting along that section of the road to be hauled out and we are suffering very much on account of the present rates. People went in there expecting that the road would have been completed and taken over a good while ago. They have cut a considerable amount of lumber, but they cannot move it out on account of the freight rates and that is a style of business "we do not like. We like a margin of profit on our work but none of us will be able to ship out our lumber till we get better freight rates. I hope the Government will make some permanent arrangement whereby we can ship out our stuff.
Of course, the hon. member understands that the Government has no power to compel the contractors to carry the freight at any special rate.
Has not the time expired during which the road was to be completed?

It is quite usual for the Government to extend the time and that has been done in this case. So far as the operation of the road is concerned, undoubtedly the Grand Trunk Pacific are the first ones that should operate that road and everything will be done to persuade that company to take it over; but if by any chance they do not do so, some other arrangement will be made for the operation of the road between Quebec and Moncton. I agree with the hon. gentleman that the lowest possible freight and passenger rates should be given, and also the very best accommodation that the rates can justify. The contractors have been urged, I myself have urged them, to finish this work as quickly as possible. The hon. member states that a certain section of the road is in first-class shape, but I may say that some of the stations and water tanks have not yet been built on that 100 miles. The contractors inform me that the road will be handed over to the commission some time in July or at the latest by the first of August. The Government will then be in a position to make an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific for the operation of the road.

I am not speaking in any fault-finding spirit, but as one of those affected. I know I am not alone and that there are a large number of lumbermen who cannot stand the high rates. My reason for bringing this matter'to the notice of the minister was that he might do everything possible to relieve the situation as quickly as possible. We are really suffering for want of reasonable Tates, and we will not get them until the road is permanently taken over by some one who will give us through rates.

Undoubtedly we need a better service from Moncton to Edmundston and from Edmundston to St. Eleuthere. At the present time a mixed train runs from Moncton to Edmundston, and although it leaves Moncton at a fixed hour you never see it back at a fixed hour. It is due at eight o'clock but never arrives until midnight or one or two in the morning. I know there is sufficient business on that line to warrant a daily train from Edmundston. From Edmundston to St. Eleuthere we have a tri-weekly service. This service is not sufficient to meet the demands of the business men, for they run a special train once in a while. They ran one or two special trains last week. I would like to see the suggestion of my hon. friend adopted and a good service established between Moncton and Levis. On the first day of August I hope we will have realized our ambition to have first-class trains running between these two points. There is a large quantity of lumber along the line of the road from Edmundston to St. Eleuthfere, and I believe that a large business could be done in the transportation of this lumber. The lumbermen living along the line have endeavoured to make some arrangement whereby round logs can be shipped from Edmundston down to St. Leonard. The road could earn a large amount of money if it could secure this business, but the management could not agree with the lumbermen as to the freight rate, and m>
arrangement was arrived at. However, I hope to see a daily service established.

I am not at all surprised to find that other members of the House have had the same experience as I have myself. It is important that this matter should be settled at once. I represent an estate and we have been trying to carry on a lumber business for the last two or three years. If we had the assurance of a satisfactory freight rate, and that we could get the lumber away, we could do business next year. But without that assurance we cannot do anything. You have to commence operations in September or October to make a success of the lumber business, and in. my own case it is absolutely necessary that-some arrangement should be made at once-I presume that that would apply to the-case of my hon. friend from Sherbrooke-(Mr. MoCrea), and every other member who has any business connection with the road. I would like to ask the minister whether there is any truth in the report that is freely circulated around the corridors that the Grand Trunk Pacific people have practically refused to take over this road and that this intimation has been received within the last week I would be very sorry to learn that it is true but I have been told that a great many times during the past week by people who are supposed to be in the confidence of Mr. Smithers, who, I understand, is now in Canada. I hope it is not true and I hope the Government will be able to assure us that steps will be taken by which the Grand Trunk Pacific will take over and operate the road. I think we need it for competition if for nothing else. Now I am going to make a suggestion to my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways and Canals. If the Grand Trunk Pacific will not take it over how would it do to try the experiment of runnljrg^a few first-class
445G

trains from Moncton to Levis, and then to Montreal, and see what the possibilities of this road would be as compared with the Intercolonial railway? If the Grand Trunk Pacific will not take it over it may be possible ehat the Government will find it of some advantage. It might be an opportunity of testing out the matter and of seeing what the time and cost would be, what the general traffic conditions are, and whether we have been justified in assuming .that a railway with a -04 grade is a cheaper road to operate than a railway with a higher grade.
This is the first time I have heard the rumour mentioned by my hon. friend that the Grand Trunk Pacific has refused to take over this portion of the road.

I am very glad to hear
it.
Yes.

-should try the experiment of running through trains, is a good one and I have no doubt that when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) is considering the matter that is a suggestion that will be acted upon.

I was surprised a moment ago to hear my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways and Canals state that the portion of the line between

the St. Lawrence and Moncton has not yet been completed. It is practically complete, although I understood him to say that there were a few new stations to be built. These should have been built long ago because they do not involve any heavy work. The public was under the impression that the road is as complete for all practical purposes as it can be. There may be a few station houses to erect and a few other things to be done but for all practical purposes we understood that the road was complete. The section from Quebec to Winnipeg is to be completed this summer, I understand.
Yes.

It is expected that the portion between Cochrane and Winnipeg will be completed in September and that between Cochrane and Quebec in November or thereabouts. There also the work can be done with absolute certainty and the road can be put in a position to be handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific, but there is this condition that has not been fulfilled-the ferry at Quebec has not been completed and may not be completed this season although I hope it will be. But whether it can be or not, it is painfully certain that the terminals at Quebec have not even been commenced. Nothing has been done for the last three years to provide a station in the city of Quebec. Three years ago nearly, when my hon. friends took office a contract was let for the building of the station. That contract was cancelled two years ago and the station which we were told was to be erected on the Champlain market has not yet been commenced. An arrangement has been made by the Grand Trunk Pacific, behind the back of the Grand Trunk, to which the Grand Trunk has not been a party, to build a union station to be used jointly by the Canadian Pacific railway and the Transcontinental railway. You cannot operate a railway without shops, and the Government have located the shops of the Grand Trunk Pacific eight miles away, without any connection with the main line. Under such conditions the Grand Trunk Pacific may say that the -line is not complete and that they will not take it. If the hon. gentleman has any information to give to the country, we will be glad to hear it, but I am afraid this is the fatal truth.
The right hon. gentleman is aware that tenders have been called for the station at Champlain market?
When?
The tenders are to be received the first week in Jnne.

That is only
for a freight station.

That is for a passenger
station.

Are yon going
to have two stations in Quebec?
There has been an arrangement come to with the Canadian Pacific railway by which we are to have joint terminals at the Palais; there is to be a union station there.
Has the Grand Trunk Pacific been consulted about that?
It has been done through the chairman of the Trane continental Railway Commission. When I mentioned the matter to Mr. Chamberlin, he made no objection to it. There is no trouble about that.
There is every trouble about that.

I always
thought the shops were to be built for the Grand Trunk Pacific and- not for the Canadian Northern.

This is an important matter and it should be thoroughly threshed out. Apparently nothing whatever has been done since last session towards having the Grand Trunk Pacific operate the sections of the line in New Brunswick which have been completed. Last session of Parliament I called attention to the fact that the portion of the line completed in New Brunswick had been operated very unsatisfactorily, and without any parliamentary authority. I also referred to the Transcontinental Railway statute under which provision was made that an agreement should be entered into with the Grand Trunk Pacific for the operation of portions of the road as they were completed from time to time, pending the completion of the whole line and the entering into a lease for the operation of the whole line. I called the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that it would be very desirable to have the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is to operate the line, enter at once upon the
operation of the completed sections, because that company being interested in making the road as profitable as possible would be interested in developing traffic, in giving accommodation to the people, and in encouraging industries along the line as any sensible railway company would do. I called the attention of the minister to the fact that previous to September, 1911, the Grand Trunk Pacific had made a propo*i* tion to the late Government to operate any sections completed, which would include the portion completed in New Brunswick, on terms mo?', favourable to the Government. They offered to operate these sections and to keep an accurate account of the receipts and operating expenses, and if there should be any deficit that the amount of that deficit should be added to capital account on which the Grand Trunk Pacific would pay interest. That was a most favourable arrangement for the country. I asked the Minister of Railways if the Government had approached the Grand Trunk Pacific since this Government came into office and invited them to enter into such an arrangement, and he said that the Government had not done so, and that they had not given consideration to the provisions of the statute 'bearing on that matter. At page 6835, * Hansard ' of last year, I said:
Mr. Pugsley : My reason for emphasising the matter is that I hope the Minister of Railways will enter into a lease with the company.
Mr. Cochrane: For the fourth time I say I shall.
And yet, it appears to-day 'that up to the present time no effort has been made to enter into an arrangement with the Grand Tunk Pacific to operate the completed sections in New Brunswick. In that respect the Government is guilty of negligence and total disregard of the interests of the country. The sections in New Brunswick are being operated by the Intercolonial railway management temporarily. The management of the Intercolonial railway has no interest in developing traffic for the Grand Trunk Pacific, which might compete with the Intercolonial. After the solemn promise made by the Minister of Railways last session, there is no excuse for the acting minister saying now that nothing has been done, that the Grand Trunk Pacific has not been approached, and that the Government has not attempted to carry out in the slightest degree the pledges made to Parliament last session. The idea the late Government had was that the Grand Trunk Pacific should begin to operate the

line down to Moncton, that they would get their running rights over the Intercolonial to Halifax and St. John, and that long before this we would have the Grand Trunk Pacific trains running from Edmundston to Moncton and on to Halifax and St. John. Had the late Government remained in power, the work on the terminals at St. John, and also at Halifax, would have been started long ago. So far back as 1910, the Grand Trunk Pacific bought some forty acres of land at the head of Courtenay bay with the view of making terminals there. They sent their engineers down, and had plans very carefully prepared, intending to begin the work of construction, but since this Government has come to power, evidently this whole matter of the operation of the eastern division of the Grand Trunk Pacific has been allowed to drift. The Grand Trunk Pacific apparently do not know where they are at so far as doing business through Maritime provinces ports is concerned, and not a thing has been done since September, 4911. That land is lying idle and not a dollar s worth of work has 'been done during the two years and nine months that this Government has been in power. What excuse can the acting minister offer for not having the promise which the minister made last session carried out? The Grand Trunk Pacific were willing four years ago to make the arrangement I have mentioned; they were willing to make it when this Government came into office, and they are willing, so far as I know, to make it now, and yet the Government pay so little attention to this matter that it has not thought it worth while to take the trouble to approach the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company on the subject.
As il have said, this delay is inexcusable. At the last session of Parliament the Government secured an appropriation of $130,000 for the purpose of building a spur from the Intercolonial to Courtenay bay, which it was supposed might be used to a certain extent by the Grand Trunk Pacific trains.; yet not a dollar of expenditure has been made. The Government came to Parliament and got the $130,000, I suppose, with a view to leading the people of St. John to believe that at last the Government was going to wake up and do something. Nevertheless, nothing has been done except to make a few surveys and to put in a few stakes. I would like the hon. minister to explain these matters to 
the House. We are now called upon to vote money; and we, who represent those people who are interested in the early operation by the Grand Trunk Pacific of these completed portions of the railway, have a right to be informed as to the reason for this apparently wholly inexcusable delay and as to the intention of the Department of Railways with regard to the matter.

So far as the operation of this portion of the road by the Grand Trunk Pacific is concerned, I remember the discussion last year with the Minister of Railways and Canals, and I have no doubt that he took the matter up with the commission and with the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Did he?
I have no doubt that he did.
I think we have a right to be informed upon that point.

I am not in a position to say definitely that he did, but I am of this opinion that the Grand Trunk Pacific are not anxious to operate that portion of the road until it is completed between Quebec and Moncton.

What grounds has my
hon. friend for believing that?
I am of the opinion that they were not very anxious to do it, for the reason that they were not anxious to operate any other portion of the road.
They offered to do this.

The hon. member states that
on his own authority. I do not know whether there was any offer in writing or not.
Mr. PUGSLEY r I stated it at the last session of Parliament.
Mr. RE'ID: My hon. friend has made the statement, tout I have never seen anything on record in the department to show that the Grand Trunk Pacific were willing to operate on the terms a3 suggested by the hon. member for St. John.

The Minister of Railways at the last .session gave his pledge to Parliament that the Grand Trunk Pacific would be asked to enter into an agreement for operating the portion of the railway in New Brunswick. Have they been approached in accordance with that promise? What has taken place, and what is their answer?
I am satisfied that, if the Minister of Railways gave that promise, he approached the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the result was that they were willing that it should be operated by the Intercolonial.
Does the acting Minister of Railways know that?
The hon. member knows that the road is being operated at a loss by the Intercolonial.
In a half-hearted way.

The hon. member states that the Intercolonial shows no interest in the development of that part of the country. So far as the Intercolonial is concerned, the Government are behind the operating of the Intercolonial and the development that may be done by that railway, and are anxious to develop not only that part but any part of Canada through which the Intercolonial runs. Therefore, if anything can be done, in so far as developing that part of the country is concerned, the Government will make the Intercolonial management do what is necessary.

I am afraid that is a pretty serious statement, namely, that you will make the Intercolonial management do anything.
Mr. REiID: Of course we will. As I understand it, a train leaves Moncton, goes up the line one day and back the next. If there were sufficient traffic to justify the operating of a daily service, or more than one train a day each way, there is no doubt at all that the management would have the necessary service put on. I understand, however, that the train that is now doing the work does not have a full load either way each day, and that, therefore, the running of more trains would only increase the loss now being suffered each month under the present service. The delay in not having the road completed is not the fault of this Government. The contracts were let some years ago. The contractors have been pushed and pressed by the commission, the Minister of Railways and Canals and myself, while I was acting during the absence of the Minister of Railways and Canals, to get them to complete the road at the earliest possible date. There are other parts of the road between Winnipeg and Quebec where the contractors have not finished their work. The original contracts were let, I think, in 1907 or 1908.

But this portion from
Edmundston to Moncton was completed long ago.
But my hon. friend is complaining that the other portion of the road between Edmundston and Quebec is not completed.

I am complaining that the portions of the road that are now completed are not being operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific in accordance with the terms of the statute. Parliament expressly provided for this several years ago, and I want to know why the Government is absolutely ignoring the provisions of the Act of Parliament. The deputy minister ought to be able to inform the acting minister whether or not, since this pledge was made to Parliament last session, the Grand Trunk Pacific has been approached with a view to operating the line between Edmundston and Moncton. If there is correspondence on the subject, it ought to be brought down; but the acting minister ought to be informed, as to why this extraordinary state of affairs exists to-day, namely, that a solemn pledge given to Parliament at the last session has been apparently wholly ignored. The acting minister does not profess to have any knowledge on the subject at all, and simply says that he believes that the Grand Trunk Pacific has been approached. His only reason for believing that is that he thinks they would not be anxious to operate the road. There is the fact which I state as an ex-minister, namely, that the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific met with my right hon. friend, then leader of the Government, the ex-Minister of Railways, ex-Minister of Finance and myself at a conference at which he distinctly offered to operate portions of the Transcontinental, as completed, on the terms which I have mentioned, so that the country would not be obliged to sustain a loss as it is doing now by the operation of the Intercolonial, but that any deficit in the operation would be charged up to capital account of the Transcontinental, and upon that the Grand Trunk Pacific would pay interest just as they are to pay interest upon the cost of the line when it is fully completed. iSurely my hon. friend should give the committee the information.	If he cannot do it now, I think this item should stand until after recess. The people of St. John, the people of New Brunswick, are anxious to see the Grand Trunk Pacific

trains coming down through the province; to realize that their expectations are about to be fulfilled and that the Grand Trunk Pacific is to operate all the eastern portions of the line as well as the western portions. They are anxious to see an enterprising corporation that is interested in the future development of the road taking hold of it and operating it. My hon. friend says the Intercolonial management would be anxious to develop traffic over the Transcontinental, because they have the Government behind them. The boast has been made that the management is to be non-political, non-partisan; and we find that, when the management does things which are horribly unpopular, which are very much against the public interest, and which have aroused the people of St. John and the people living all along the line of the Intercolonial, and made it so that, if the people could realize that the Government are responsible for what the management has done, the Government would not be able to get any support in the counties through which the Intercolonial runs, the Government hide themselves behind the statement that the management is independent of the Government and that the Government is not responsible. Take that famous-or infamous-agreement between Mr. Gutelius, the general manager of the Intercolonial, and Mr. Bosworth of the Canadian Pacific railway. That matter was put up to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ha^en) in St. John. His friends* apologized; they said: It is an outrageous and indefensible agreement; but Mr. Hazen had nothing to do with it; it was done behind his back; Mr, Gutelius had power to do what he liked, and neither Mr. Hazen nor the Government could prevent that outrageous agreement coming into operation. I say' the management of the Intercolonial is entirely opposed to the development of traffic upon the Transcontinental, if you look upon it as a business proposition, because the Transcontinental is going to compete with the Intercolonial.
Whose fault is that?

It is nobody's 'fault.'
It is to the credit of the late Government, for the reason that it gives competition. We want the Transcontinental to compete with the Intercolonial and hope that the result of having the two roads will be to give to the people advantages which they did not enjoy before. I might as well ask the Post-

master General whose ' fault ' it was that the Canadian Pacific railway was built from St. John to Montreal. We had the Intercolonial before, and it was the ' fault ' of the Government, but very much to their credit, that this competition was established with the advantages it involved in competitive rates and otherwise.
Does the hon. gentleman, say that the National Transcontinental give's competitive rates?
It will.
Not at all.

Of course it will. Today it does not give competitive rates, nor a competitive service; it gives a wretched service, one that is entirely- unsatisfactory. But what we want

I presume that the people in the various portions of the Dominion where sections of this road are completed are alike in wanting it-is to get the Grand Trunk Pacific at work, to get competition, to get them interested in the development of eastern Canada. The day when the Grand Trunk Pacific trains go through the central part of the province to Moncton and St. John and Halifax the people will have new heart and new hope, because they will see that a new day has dawned. The Intercolonial is ignoring the Grand Trunk Pacific and is giving this wretched and inefficient service.

The acting Minister of Railways said that there was still some work to be done to complete the section from Edmundston to Moncton, tnat there were a number of station houses to be built. Could he give us information now .as to how many station houses are tp be built, and when they will be completed?

I have not that information, but I will have it before we go through any of the Transcontinental Estimates. The information I have as to the condition of the road is gained in part from discussing with the contractors two or three times within the last month or two the question when the road will be ready to hand over to the commission. The contractors stated that they expected to get to work about the 1st of May, and that there would be about two months' work in finishing up a number of little things that are to be completed. I will have the details when we meet after dinner.

Will the hon. gentleman also bring the information I asked for?

iMr. REID: Yes. I have no objection to this item standing, but there is another item as to the operating of the road, and-
Bnt will the hon. gentleman himself keep it in mind?
There is this other item of the operation of the line from Moncton to Levis.
This is just as good.
I have no objection to letting this item stand.
We want to know what communication has been had with the Grand Trunk Pacific?

I want to say a few words before we leave this item. Do I understand the acting minister to say that if the Grand Trunk Pacific does not take over the operation of this line from Edmundston to Levis, it will fall into the hands of the Intercolonial railway management?

What I said was that if the Grand Trunk Pacific refuses to take it over, then it falls into the hands of the Government to arrange for its operation in some other way. It could be put under the management of the Intercolonial railway, or an arrangement could be made with some other parties to operate it.

On what ground would the Grand Trunk Pacific refuse to operate it? Oould it be on any other ground than that the Government has departed from the contract, has degraded the eastern section of the Transcontinental and has made changes without the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific? Certainly it is a curious thing for the acting minister to suggest the possibility that they might refuse to operate it. It is rather an argument in support of the view that he knows that the Government has departed from the terms of the contract and has given the Grand Trunk Pacific the excuse which we have always urged they would have in consequence of the changes made.

The hon. gentleman knows
that if the Grand Trunk absolutely refused to take over the operation of this portion until the whole road is completed, they may do so, as I understand the terms of the contract. Of course, the hon. member is a shrewd lawyer and understands the legal position better than I do, but I think he will agree that we cannot compel them to
take this portion of the road from Moncton to Levis by itself. So, if the Government approached the Grand Trunk Pacific and tried to make an arrangement concerning this portion of the road, which is what we would naturally do, and if we could not make an arrangement with them that we could justify to this Douse, surely, we must take some other means of operating this portion of the line.
Has the hon. gentleman tried to make any other arrangement?

I do not think it is the
proper time-not until the road is ready to be operated.
The whole road?
No, this portion.

But the portion from
Moncton to Edmundston-
Mr. 'REID:	I speak of the road from
Quebec to Moncton. The hon. member is getting back to the part between Edmundston and Moncton. We agreed that that was to stand until after dinner, when 1 shall have the information to answer him.

I am not through. I want to add a few words. I am sorry the hon. acting minister cannot understand me in French, but I will do the best I can to say what I mean in English. I wish to protest at once against the idea of having this part of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the hands of the Intercolonial railway. We have heard too much in this House and outside about this American, Mr. Gute-lius-

He is not an American, he
is a Canadian citizen.

He is a Canadian
now, but I do not think that he will ever forget that he was an American.
He has been eighteen years in this country.

He is paid $20,000 a
year for the management of the Intercolonial railway. You cannot get it out of the minds of people outside of this House that Mr. Gutelius is under pay by the Canadian Pacific railway to let the Canadian Pacific railway profit by every pound of freight that can be diverted from the Intercolonial railway to the Canadian Pacific railway. On my responsibility as a member, I say that you cannot take that out of the minds of the people, that Mr. COMMONS
Gutelius is under pay by the Canadian Pacific railway, by special fund, to work for the benefit of the Canadian Pacific railway. I know that is a strong accusation, but I say it is in the minds of the public, and you cannot get it out of their minds. If Mr. Gutelius is going to have the management of that part of the National Transcontinental railway, we shall not see that part from Edmundston to Levis in operation inside of two, three, four or five years; why? Because, as long as the traffic comes up from Moncton to Edmundston by the National Transcontinental railway, it must go on from Edmundston by the Canadian Pacific railway. Having in mind what Mr. Gutelius could do for the Canadian Pacific railway, he will do his best to keep that part from Edmundston to Levis closed to traffic. More than that, we need only to read the conclusion of his report to see that he has condemned that part from Levis to Moncton, and even the assistant to the Minister of Railways has adhered to that part of Mr. Gutelius' report, that this part of the road should not have been constructed because it would interfere with the Intercolonial. I for one-and I hope I will be joined by some hon. members through whose ridings that part of the Transcontinental runs-I see the hon. member for LTslet in his place, and I hope he will join me in protesting against that man being allowed to put his hands on the Transcontinental from Edmundston to Levis. It is his duty to the public to do so, if he wants uiat road to serve properly the constituency that sends him here. He snould stand up and say: I want this road to be operated as soon as possible, not by Mr. Guteiius, but by the Government.

As I stated, when the road is completed between Quebec and Moncton, which will be within a couple of months, the Government will do all they can to give satisfactory arrangements, which they can justify, with the Grand Trunk Pacific. It should first be approached to operate this road; but if we cannot make an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific, then an arrangement may be made -with the Intercolonial railway, and a satisfactory service will be given. If the road is operated between Quebec and Moncton by the Intercolonial railway, or under any other arrangement that may be made by the Government, a satisfactory service will be given. I do not think that the Minister of Railways could do anything more than I have suggested.

I think it is my
bounden duty not only to protest against what has been said by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau), but, as far as possible, to prevent the people from being induced to believe what some of our friends on the other side-and our friend from Timiscouata is to the forefront in that respect-

I boast of it.
Mr. PELLETIER-are trying to make the people of the country believe that we have, in the manager of the Intercolonial railway, an enemy of this country who. is bound, hand and foot, to the Canadian Pacific railway.
Hear hear.
-and wdio is protecting the Canadian Pacific railway against the interests of this country. I want to protest emphatically against such an accusation.

How do you know?
How can you say?
If my hon. friend will wait a minute I will show-
Come down and tell the people about it.
Sit down.
Who said sit down?

If the hon. member has anything more to say I am quite willing-
It is your friend beside you who says, sit down, I want to know who it is. Oh, yes, it is the hon. member for Chambly (Mr. Rainville). He is not worthy of the name.

A movement has been been started in the province of Quebec, all along the Intercolonial railway, which I think ought to be condemned. It is to the effect that in order to gain
5 p.m. political advantage, to try to make the people of our country believe that we have appointed as manager of the Intercolonial railway an American, to use the word which my hon. friend has used. This gentleman is not an American. His interest has been with this country for eighteen years, and he is at the present moment trying to do his level best for the Intercolonial railway. I have risen not to defend Mr. Gutelius
You cannot.

-but to enter my strong protest and to tell this House at this very opportune moment that I have had occasion to test the feelings of Mr. Gutelius as between his duty and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; and I am going to give that experience to the House now. If it can put a stop to the things that are being said against Mr. Gutelius and render some justice to him, I shall be happy in having done so. When, as Postmaster General, I was confronted with the demands of the railway companies of Canada for an increase in the amount which they received for the transportation of the mails of this country, and when I had the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk, the Quebec Central, the Canadian Northern railway and other companies uniting to. try to get from this country an increase of $4,000,000, so that they would have $6,000,000 altogether instead of the $2,000,000 which they had been receiving,
I was obliged to have recourse to somebody who knew (something about these matters. I went to my colleague and friend the Minister of Railways and asked him if he could not give me somebody who would help me from a railway point of view to ascertain what the -cost of the transportation of the mails was and to try to strike the best bargain possible for Canada. Who is the man whom Mr. Cochrane gave me for that purpose? He gave me Mr. Gutelius.
Sure.

And Mr. Gutelius stood by the Post Office Department, stood by the interests of this country, and put before us , figures which could not 'be controverted by the Canadian Pacific railway. He fought the battle of the Post Office Department and of the country against the Canadian Pacific railway. If I have been able to settle with the railways on the basis oi ;$780,000 a year increase instead of the $4,000,000 which the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk demanded, a debt of gratitude is due to Mr. Gutelius who helped me to accomplish that. When last year a question arose about what road was to transport the ocean mails during the winter season, the Canadian Pacific railway did their best to secure that contract; but Mr. Gutelius fought the battle of the Intercolonial railway and was able to induce the Post Office Department to send the mails by the Intercolonial railway as
against the Canadian Pacific railway. Tnese are two points that may tend to prevent these-I cannot say calumnies, but if I were speaking of any person outside of the House I would say that Mr. Gutelius, for political purposes, was being calumniated.
I think the Postmaster General will receive the gratitude of Mr. Gutelius in the next general election, and he will need it.

I may need it less
than you.

As to the accusations brought forward against Mr. Gutelius, I am here representing a part of the public. Not only have I heard statements myself, but I have received many letters from citizens, not only of my riding, but of other ridings, and from many men on the Intercolonial, prominent men of both parties, asking me if I could ascertain really whether Mr. Gutelius was not under pay by the Canadian Pacific railway to make business for the Canadian Pacific railway against the Intercolonial railway, The Postmaster (General knows something about Quebec and the feeling in the ridings \ through which the Intercolonial railway runs. He knows that nearly half the men employed on the Intercolonial railway were laid off last winter, and many of them without a single day's notice. And why? Because the traffic from Moncton and St. John had been handed over by Mr. Gutelius to the Canadian Pacific railway instead of to the Intercolonial railway. The Postmaster General will hear something about that at the next general election, and I am sure that in my county and in his own county he will be told that the people of Temis-couata think the same as the hon. member for Temiseouata. I hope the hon. member for L'lalet will speak out some day and tell the Postmaster General that the same feeling prevails in his riding. We all know he is a great admirer of the Postmaster General because one day he said that the Postmaster General was worthy to wear the mantle of Sir George Cartier, and if he wants to be fair and frank he will advise [DOT] him to see to it.
Item stands.
Quebec bridge-construction, $3,000,000.

Can the minister say
approximately when the Quebec bridge will be completed?

In 1917.
Hudson bay railway-construction of railway terminals and elevators, $4,500,000.

Will the minister give the House a statement as to present conditions and future prospects in regard to construction, and in regard to the terminal at Port Nelson which, I understand, is under his department.

Does the Government
allow subcontractors on that line?

So far as I know there are no subcontractors. I think McArthur is doing the work himself. Bails have been laid for nearly 110 miles, and the road has been graded for 158 miles. Bails will be laid on the newly graded portion within the next two or three months. The right of way has been cleared as far as Split lake, and the contractors are proceeding with the work as quickly as possible.
How far is Split lake from Le Pas?

The distance is 253 miles,
and from Split lake to Port Nelson is 165 miles.
What is the condition of the work up to the 158 mile point and from there on to Split lake?

The right of way has been
cleared and partly graded.
Is the work in hand all the way to Split lake? My hon. friend says the work is all being done by one contractor but he might be working within a mile or two of the end of the graded portion.

The whole road up to Split
lake is under way, and the contractors expect to complete that portion of the road this year.
Will rails be laid to Split lake this summer?
Yes.
Split lake is at the first crossing, is it not?
Manitou Portage is the first crossing.
How far is that from Split lake?

I do not seem to have the
distance here, but I can get it for the hon-gentleman.

I only wanted the best
available information. There will be two-bridges across the Nelsion river. Will there be any delay in connection with the erection of those bridges? Has the material for these bridges been ordered?

There will be no delay. The
contract includes the substructure for these bridges. Plans are already being prepared and the contracts will be let as soon as possible, so there will be no delay in connection with the bridges.
Have they started work on the substructure of the bridges yet?
I do not think so. Nothing has been done in so far as the permanent substructure at the crossing is concerned. It is only a temporary work in the meantime.
Do I understand grading *work is now progressing from the first crossing of the Nelson?
Yes.

I was talking with the contractor, and also with the chief engineer, while in Winnipeg at Easter, and they assured me that they will have steel laid to Nelson by the fall of 1915. They figure it out that they will reach Manitou, the first crossing of the Nelson river, with steel this fall.
What is the mileage to the crossing from Le Pas?

Something over 280 miles-. They have a lot of the grading and a good deal of the rock cutting done now between where steel is at present1 and the first crossing of the Nelson river. They will reach the first crossing of the Nelson river this fall.

With the steel?
Mr. SH'AEPE: With the steel. They will put up the bridge during the winter. The grading will be done between the two crossings of the Nelson river during this summer so that the moment spring opens up they will be able to run the steel from one crossing to the other. During next spring they will put up the second bridge,.

and the following summer they will go right into Port Nelson.
Are the bridges across the Nelson serious engineering matters?

They are large works.
iMr. REID: They are large bridges, but *not serious as far as the engineering is concerned. .
They figure on taking part of the substructure up over lake Winnipeg, and that way before they reach the first crossing of the Nelson with the steel.
I understand that there is a wireless station at Port Nelson, so that the department will be in direct communication with it all the time?
Yes.
Has the season sufficiently advanced at Port Nelson to allow work to begin there yet?

We have had a large number of men employed there all winter at the terminals, and the reports we get are that everything is going along satisfactorily as far as the terminals are concerned. The men were kept busy all winter, and the latest reports were that the ice would be *out of the river before the end of the present month. The chief engineer told me that the reports that he got from Mr. McLaughlin, the engineer in charge there, were that everything was going along very well.	,
Is there any news about the dredge which was said to have been wrecked last fall?
The dredge is all right, and they will proceed with the dredging as soon as the ice is out of the river.
It was reported that the dredge was on the ground and its back broken.

There was no truth in that report. They ran the dredge on the beach for the winter, and she was perfectly safe. She*-was just laid up in that way for the winter. The report is that everything is all right as far as the dredge is concerned.
There were one or two vessels wrecked. What is the final story in regard to these vessels and their cargoes ?

There was one boat called the Allette that arrived at Nelson all right but, the captain or the crew, as I understand,
allowed the vessel to drift a little and damaged her. The vessel started to come back with part of her cargo, but they decided that it was better to return. They were probably afraid they would not get out and they beached the vessel on the shore and she took fire. I think they were able to put the fire out and save nearly all of the cargo. The vessel, of course, was in a damaged condition. I suppose she has been abandoned to the underwriters. There was another steamer called the Cearense. I think the crew were not careful enough in taking soundings while trying to enter the harbour, and they ran her on a shoal and abandoned her. According to the reports I have, the vessel is there just in the same condition as when they abandoned her; they are taking the cargo out of her, and there will be no loss as far as the Government is concerned.
Has any claim been made against the Government on account of these wrecks?
No. The Government had the cargoes, and the cargoes were insured, so that the Government lost nothing. The Government were not responsible for the vessels.
No claim has been made.

What is the programme of work at Port Nelson for the summer? Seme time ago I asked the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or the Minister of Railways, what the scheme of improvement was and what it was likely to cost. I was not able to get the information at that time. Could the minister now say what it is proposed to do at Port Nelson and what it is expected to cost to make it a satisfactory port?

The work being proceeded with there is the construction of about a mile and a half of pier out into deep water, so that vessels can come alongside the pier, discharge and take on cargoes. That is a considerable work in itself.
A mile and a half out?
The pier work will extend out into deep water and will then run a mile and a half along the shore.

To what depth?
446(5
Thirty-five feet.
I understand the pier will run a mile and a half along the shore, and then how far from the shore will it extend until it reaches a depth of thirty-five feet.
It is a short distance from the shore to deep water.

The minister means
thirty-five feet at low water?
Yes.
Why is the pier to run a mile and a half along the shore? Why not carry the track along the dry land until it reaches the pier extending out to deep water?
The pier runs diagonally out into deep water, and it is expected that there will be a lot of business, and that we will require extensive piers and terminals at that particular point.
How many miles of dredging will there be and what will be the width and depth of the channel to be created?

It is hardly correct to say
that any number of miles of dredging will be necessary. The channel is all right now for light draught steamers of eighteen or twenty feet, but on the completion of the railway large steamers are expected, and dredging will be necessary. The channel should be at least 300 feet wide.

The minister is courteous but not definite. I was under the impression that a great deal of dredging would be necessary at Port Nelson to make that harbour available for traffic, and my impression was that the total cost would run into the millions. I take it for granted that before the Government decided to establish Port Nelson as the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway they satisfied themselves as to what the cost would be. If the Government has no definite information as to the work required to be done there and the cost of it, then it was premature in deciding on the terminus.

Last year the minister explained that he had sent Mr. Hazen, an engineer, to look over the whole situation at Churchill and Nelson, and Mr. Hazen reported in favour of Nelson as the terminus of the railway. The minister himself went to Hudson bay and he also came to the conclusion that Nelson should be the port. The hon. gentleman will understand that as we have to depend on wireless com-

munication for our information from there, I am not able to give the House that information to which it is entitled. The hon. gentleman would be justified in coming to the conclusion that there would be a great deal of dredging at Nelson were it not for the fact that we are building the piers out to deeper water in order to save dredging. My information is that there is not so much dredging to be done as the general public-seem to think.

The Government has undertaken a serious responsibility, and if they can tell the House how much work is to be done and what it will cost, the people, will know what merit there is in the enterprise. I am bound to assume, from what the minister has said, that he is not in a position to say how much dredging is necessary to make the port satisfactory, or how much that dredging will cost.
Is there any report from Mr. Hazen or from any one else which shows what kind of material has to be-dredged?
The report shows that it isclay, not rock.	.
Is it not sand?
Some of it is sand but it is mostly clay.

I have been informed
by seafaring mem and by experienced officers of vessels who have been there that it. is largely sand and that it will require continuous dredging to keep a channel open.

Had the sand been lodging,
there every year, there would hardly be any channel left now, but there is a channel into Nelson, and a very good one, except at a few places where it is said the clay will have to be dredged.

I understand the ships
are to anchor out a long distance from the harbour.
They go in opposite Nelson.
The usual condition with sand in such cases is that you will always have a channel some place, but it will be continually changing its position and is not reliable.

Last year a certain number of men were hired in Nova Scotia to work at Port Nelson in connection with the terminals, and it was under-

stood by the men that their wages were to be paid to their wives, and for that purpose powers of attorney were duly executed, and as I understand, left with the Bank of Montreal at Halifax.
I am sorry I cannot avail myself of some papers which I have in my possession in relation to this matter, but unfortunately I cannot put my hands upon them at the moment. The fact that these wages were not paid promptly by some officials of the Railway Department caused a great deal of want on the part of the families of the men who were in the Government service at Hudson bay, and to whose families the Government had promised promptly to pay these men's wages. It is hardly worth while my detailing to the ex-minister the vast amount of suffering that this has brought about. Families were actually broken up at Halifax on this account. I know of a case where one family was left without a home, and in other cases public subscriptions had to be taken up to keep the families of some of these men from actual want. One case of delayed wages was called to my attention last summer by a friend of one of the interested parties, and I wired the Minister of Railways. The department took the matter up very promptly with some officials of the department at Winnipeg. Later on the money canne to the party on whose account I had communicated with the Minister of Railways, and I discovered that this matter had been absolutely neglected by everybody until the attention of the department had been called to it by me. I am not exaggerating the deprivation and the want that these delays 'brought about. This matter has been woefully and disgracefully neglected by somebody. I do not say it was the fault of the minister, but it was the fault of some one.
Further let me say this, in regard to the men engaged in the work at Port Nelson last season. A contract in writing was entered into between them and the Department of Railways, in which agreement the amount of wages which they were to receive was specifically stated. The men were dissatisfied with the conditions under which they were working and claimed-whether correctly or not I do not know-that the Department of Railways was violating its contract, and they still so claim. Many of them left Port Nelson and returned to their homes in Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and elsewhere. A large number of them later on associated themselves together
in order to press their claims against the Department of Railways for moneys which they said were improperly retained by the department, and their claims were put into the hands of a solicitor for prosecution against the Department of Railways. It was necessary for them to proceed by petition of right and to receive a fiat from the Department of Justice. The petition asking for leave to commence action has been before the Department of Justice now for many months, and I understand that the solicitor for the applicants has yet received no satisfactory Teply from the Department of Justice or from the Department of Railways. I have been advised' by the Minister of Railways himself that the delay is due to the Department of Railways, he giving the reason that he wanted some direct and positive information which he could obtain only from some of his officers at Port Nelson, and that he was awaiting that information. That may be a very good reason or it may not; I do not know; but what I want to ask the acting Minister of Railways to do is this, that he take a little interest in the matter andjook into it promptly and seriously; or if he does not propose doing so, that he call the attention of the Minister of Railways, who, I understand, has resumed his duties, to this matter. I want to assure the minister and the acting minister that, although it may appear a trivial and inconsequential matter to the department and departmental officers, yet it is quite a serious matter and one of much consequence to the parties interested. I am willing now to leave the matter in the hands of the minister, if I can have, not the ordinary perfunctory promise that he will take it into consideration, but his promise that he will direct that some person in his department will take the matter up in a businesslike and expeditious way and dispose of it one way or the other.

I would like to bring
to the attention of the minister a case which has to do with the hiring of the men at Hudson bay, but which is somewhat dissimilar to that stated by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). A number of workmen, who were engaged under contract to work at Hudson bay for a. year, accordingly went there and began work. I understand there was some difference between the labourers and officials in charge of the Government work as to the

[DOT]duties which the workmen were to perform, and as a consequence a large number of the men quit work and asked to be sent home.
One case in particular of which I have heard was that of a man who was engaged as engineer, and who claims that, when this difference among the men developed, he was along with them ordered to be sent home. He did not object so strongly to that; but he found, when he came to get his pay, that he was docked $100 for his passage from Hudson bay to Halifax. Representations were immediately made to the department to have that amount of money refunded. Had he refused to work at Hudson bay, he says he would have no complaint and would not expect to have his passage money refunded; hut under the [DOT]circumstances, not having been consulted as to whether or not he was to continue to work, but having been told by the officials to pack up and go home, he claims he has a right to this $109. I have brought the matter to the attention of the department; I can quite understand, in view of the fact that the department is in touch with Hudson bay only by wireless, that such matters in the rush may be left over, but I would ask that this matter which is, as the hon. member for Halifax has said, a serious matter to la/bouring men, should receive attention as early as possible. It is simply a matter of fact to determine whether his story is correct or not, and I think the representation that this matter be investigated . and an early decision be arrived at is most reasonable and should have immediate attention.

I am glad the hon. members have brought this matter up. As I understand it, a written contract was entered into between these men to go to Port Nelson, and they went there on certain terms. These men returned after having been there for a very short time, and the result was that the' steamer by which they returned made a charge to the Government for the return fares of these men. The department, having a contract with these men and being without any information from Port Nelson, felt that they had violated that contract, and therefore $100 was retained from each of their wages towards the payment of their return fares. Representations were made to the department and came before me from the men at this end that the fault was not theirs, as has been mentioned by both hon. members who have spoken on this matter. But

it has been impossible for me to get any information from Nelson-for the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) to get such information, for the matter was brought before him, of course, prior to his leaving his office. The wireless was not working until late in the winter, and since that time I have been trying to get some further information in order so that we might decide how these claims should be disposed of. But we will have that information at the earliest possible moment, and if the fault is in any way that of the officials of the department, the claims certainly will be paid. On the other hand, if the men refused to carry out their contracts, it is hardly fair that the Government should be expected not only to pay for their time and expenses but also all tlieir claims. The matter has not been delayed in any way by the department or by the Minister of Railways and Canals.

Why not give
these men the right to bring an action against the department if they want to?

The only reason, I suppose, why they should be held for a little time is that, if we could get the information and if it were to turn out that the claims were good-that the fault was with the department-the matter could be settled without going to the courts. On the other hand, if the claims did go to the courts, we should need evidence from Nelson, and so it would be almost impossible to get the claims through the courts at an earlier time than within the next month or two. I am in hopes that we can get the information that wiil enable us to settle this matter without going to the courts.
Mr. MoKENZIsE: I have a somewhat similar line of complaint from men who were engaged by the Government in connection with the work at Hudson hay. The claim is that of four seamen of Montreal who happened to put the case in my hands in Sydney last fall. It is an easy matter for the Government to deprive a few poor men of money that is coming to them. If a sailor gets into trouble with an ordinary shipmaster, there is a certain line laid down by the law of the land for him to follow in order to get his money. But the Government can shelter itself behind its ability to refuse the seamen the opportunity of suing. For that reason more care should be taken on the part of the department, I should say, to maintain true relations between themselves and their

employees in matters of this nature, that the country and representatives of the minister may not take undue advantage of the disabilities of seamen.
The case which I wish to present to the minister is not that of foreign seamen, although foreign seamen would have just the same rights as natives of Canada. These men, at least some of them, were bom and bred in the city of Montreal, and gentlemen in this House must know them, because they have given to me the name of the wards in the city of Montreal where they live, and some of them gave me the names of the members who represent their wards in this House. I therefore bring the case to the notice of the minister, with the hope that some remedies will be granted to these men.
In the first place, I would point out that there is a difference between the means by which the Government employs seamen and that by which the ordinary masters employ them. When men are employed by the Government there is a certain course to be followed, a certain book known as the Government shipping book, in which the names of these men are entered. They are not to go through the form of signing articles, as they do in joining to an ordinary ship. But, in the case of the official of the department who engaged these men, he did not choose to follow that course. The ship had no book, as is provided for in chapter 111 of the Revised Statutes-chapter 113 is the Shipping Act which provides the mode under which seamen are ordinarily engaged. These men were employed to all intents and purposes under the ordinary articles. I have copies of the articles which they signed, the ordinary, every-day shipping articles. These men were hired by a gentleman by the name of Jones, who was master of the vessel, the Port Nelson. These men signed in the ordinary way and first joined the ship at $2 a day, with the understanding that they should be paid their fares back to the city of Montreal if the master should not take them north. When they got to the port of North Sydney, he found that he could not get other seamen, and made a further agreement with them to take them to Hudson bay at $2 a day. After they had been under that agreement for a couple of days, but before the ship left, the master discovered that he could get other men who probably suited him better, and he immediately discharged these poor men. When they asked him to pay 282
their way back to Montreal according to his agreement, he refused to do so. There was nothing left for these men to do but to bring action. They brought action in a competent court in the town of North Sydney, and after hearing the captain and the men, under the ordinary shipping agreement the court gave judgment in favour of the men for a certain amount of money-I think it was $76. What did the captain, do? The ordinary captain, I think, would have communicated with the Government and found what was to be done. The ordinary master of a privately-owned vessel would have communicated with the owners and found out whether he was authorized to pay the men or not. But this gentleman who represents this Government took these poor men and put them in jail on some pretext, saying they were trying to desert. And while they were in jail, without a trial, he put out of port, got up steam on his craft and started for Hudson bay, leaving the poor men in jail. After they had been in jail over Sunday [DOT]-for he had cleared out on Sunday-these men were brought before a stipendiary magistrate, Mr. Archibald, a very eminent gentleman, a K.C., and a gentleman who knows his business well, when the men came before him, he found that there was nobody to sustain the charge, so there was nothing left for him to do but discharge them. Then they were left wandering about until they got another position. But they were without their money and they are without it to-day so far as the Government is concerned. What did the Government do in the matter? They never inquired into the facts, so far as I know, as to whether these men had carried out their part of the arrangement and whether they had done the work they were engaged to do or not. The Government simply took advantage of the fact that the men were in the service of the Government and should have been engaged under chapter 111 of the Revised Statutes instead of being hired under chapter 113. They certioraried the case and took it up to Halifax, and the judge there held, merely on the technical point, that the men were really in the employ of the Government and should have been hired under chapter 111, and decided that the court had no jurisdiction. As to that decision the judge did not go into the merits. But the judge held, upon facts, that these men had earned their money, that they had not been paid, and should be paid. What I want to point out is that while technically they



should have been hired in under chapter 111, as I have said, they were hired in the other way. It was not their fault. They were not aware that there was any difficulty about it; there was no course open to them except the course they followed. They went into court and got judgment, and that judgment is still outstanding. This Captain Jones who had put these men in jail and left them there, came back after a while, and it wias supposed that there would be some remedy when he got to North Sydney and that the men would be paid. But this distinguished gentleman, the most respectable officer, from the time he came to North Sydney, wa3 in hiding somewhere so that the men could not do anything with him, and so these poor sailors were obliged to leave the country.
Now, the- minister may say: Captain Jones says one thing 'and the men another, and we have the right to believe Captain Jones. But I would submit that there is not much conflict as to the facts between the men and the captain-hardly any at all. They say they were to be paid their way hack to Montreal; the captain says they were not.
It is admitted in evidence by the captain that two others who were in the same crew had their way paid back to Montreal. There were six. He paid the way of two back to Montreal, but refused to pay the way of the other four, and they were stranded. The captain says in his sworn testimony, which I have here, that he paid the way of two of these men and that he would have paid the way of the other men, hut that they were not as good men as he thought they ougt to be. That is a question of opinion between the men and the captain; but here is the evidence that they performed the services and were not paid. There is the further consideration that he engaged those men to go to Hudson bay. A copy of the agreement is here, which was signed by the captain and the four men. They were four days in the vessel waiting to start out, but on the expiry of the four days he dismissed them without the slightest reason, except that he had got the other men that he was looking for. I do not know whether the minister is familiar with the Shipping Act, but it contains a provision governing dealings with sailors which says that if you hire a seaman and discharge him before he has been a month on the vessel he is entitled to a month's pay. These men were taken on and hired to go to Hudson bay. They were aboard the vessel for four days, ready

to go out; but before the ship started they were told that they were discharged. In any case, under our Shipping Act, they would be entitled to a month's pay. I submit that they are entitled to no less favourable treatment from the Government than they would have received from an ordinary shipowner. This being a question of fact, and the minister having had no opportunity of hearing the facts from the parties, I shall have to read to him briefly after eight o'clock the testimony of the captain taken under oath and the testimony of the men, with the hope that I shall make such a case before him as will enable him to see his way clear to pay these men. They are not like men who have gone beyond jurisdiction, they are still in this country.
At six o'clock the House resumed, and then took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: NORTH SHORE POWER, RAILWAY AND NAVIGATION COMPANY.
speechtext: The word ' Limited ' is not used in connection with this company, I see.

subtopic: NORTH SHORE POWER, RAILWAY AND NAVIGATION COMPANY.
speechtext:
This company,
which was originally incorporated by a private Bill, carries on business in Quebec and employs about 800 men. They wish to extend their operations outside of Quebec.

subtopic: NORTH SHORE POWER, RAILWAY AND NAVIGATION COMPANY.
speechtext: Although railway companies never use the word ' Limited ' after their names, limited liability commercial companies always do, and as the name of this railway company is being changed to the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company, the word ' Limited ' should be added in accordance with universal custom. Under the Joint Stock Act the word ' Limited ' must be added to the names of all commercial companies, and so particular is Parliament that it requires that they shall use the word in all thedr advertisements and signs so that the public will know that they are limited liability companies. I think my hon. friend will see that it is desirable that the word ' Limited ' shall be added.

subtopic: NORTH SHORE POWER, RAILWAY AND NAVIGATION COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not see any objection to that.

subtopic: NORTH SHORE POWER, RAILWAY AND NAVIGATION COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's objection is sound provided a company is incorporated by letters patent under a general Act. Then, as the hon. gentleman said, it is necessary to give notice to the public by using the word ' Limited.' But this company was incorporated by Act of Parliament, and there is no more need for using the word * Limited ' in this case than in the case of a railway or other great undertaking. This Bill was dealt with thoroughly toy the committee and it was also before the Senate Committee and 2821
no objection was made; in fact, the Bill went through the committee unanimously. If we make any change now it will probably involve laying it over till next session, as there is hardly time to have any amendments agreed to by the Senate. I have never heard the objection taken before in this House that the word ' Limited ' should be affixed to the name of a company incorporated by Act of Parliament. The hon. gentleman is quire correct in saying that a limited liability company must use the word ' Limited ' in its name if it is incorporated under any general Act. The same may be said about the companies incorporated by the legislatures in the various provinces. I know of no case where the word ' Limited ' is used. It is used as an affix to the name of any company incorporated under the general Act by letters patent.

subtopic: NORTH SHORE POWER, RAILWAY AND NAVIGATION COMPANY.
speechtext: Can my hon. friend point out any Act which has been passed in recent years incorporating a commercial or manufacturing company without having the word ' limited ' added? There is the same reason for adding the word ' limited ' where the incorporation is by Act of Parliament as where it is by letters patent. This is a company which might have been incorporated, leaving out the railway part of it, by letters patent. They chose to drop all the provisions of the Bill as far as the railway part of it is concerned and they come and ask Parliament to change their name and define their powers, which are simply those of a manufacturing and trading company. The powers which they ask could have been conferred equally well under the Joint Stock Companies Act. If there is any reason for requiring companies incorporated under that Act to have the word * limited ' after the name, the same reason applies if they choose to disregard the provisions of the Companies Act and come to Parliament for incorporation. I do not think my hon. friend can find any case in recent years of Parliament incorporating a manufacturing or commercial company with that word left out. I recognize that an amendment would have to receive one or two days' notice, but with the unanimous consent of the committee the change which I suggest might be made. My hon. friend (Mr. S. Sharpe) is the chairman of the committee, and I would like to hear his opinion with regard to that.

subtopic: NORTH SHORE POWER, RAILWAY AND NAVIGATION COMPANY.
speechtext:
I was not present when this Bill was considered by the com-

mittee, but I understand that the president and general manager of the company were present and desired the name that is in the Bill. I think my hon. friend is in error when he says that no private companies have been incorporated without the word ' limited ' being put after their names.
