speechtext: I said private companies for manufacturing or commercial, purposes.

The Prudential Trust
Company of Montreal is the Prudential Trust Company, Limited. I think all the trust companies have the word ' limited ' after their names.

I was present in
the committee when the Bill was passed and temporarily acted as chairman in the absence of the chairman and that is why I rose to my feet a moment ago. speechtext: I suppose it did not come up at all?	.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is
quite right, it did not come up at all. The name of the company is an unusual one, which is not likely to be confused with the name of any other company-the Gulf Pulp and Paper Company. It is doing business under this name in the province of Quebec. Amongst all the loan companies incorporated by this Parliament, I

have not in my mind at the present moment any case where the word 'limited' was used. I have seen many loan companies incorporated in the last ten years, and I can recall no company with the word 'limited' affixed to the name. Nor can I recall a similar use of the word 'limited' in the case of the incorporation of any trading company. I think it would be unfortunate if this Bill were thrown out, because the president of the company, who was before the committee, stated that he had an investment of $5,000,000, and that for five months in the year operations were held up because of their not being able to -make shipments after the close of navigation. speechtext: I really cannot see why we should bother about the matter, for the reason that the word 'limited' was put in the Joint Stock Companies Act for the protection of the shareholders, to notify the world at large that there was no personal liability on the part of the shareholder. My hon. friend is
entirely in erroT as to my position. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LABRADOR, QUEBEC AND SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The Senate amendments have 'been reported by the Railway Committee, with the recommendation that the first amendment be not agreed to, because it appears to tacitly admit that Newfoundland has rights along the Labrador coast, which it is not desirable for this Parliament to admit; and that the second amendment be agreed to in the following consequential amendment: substitute the Quebec Railway, Light and Power Company for the Quebec Railway, Light, Heat and Power Company.

subtopic: LABRADOR, QUEBEC AND SOUTHERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
When this Bill was before the House exception was taken to it by the Prime Minister, the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), that its passage as worded might raise some doubt on the questions before the courts as to the respective rights of Canada and Newfoundland in Labrador. The Senate amended the Bill, by saying that the works of the company are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, and the Railway Committee having reported on the amendments, I beg to move:
That order No. 58 be discharged, and that the said Bill be withdrawn and the fees paid thereon be refunded.
Section 8 of the Bill reads as follows:
The company may lay out, construct and operate a railway of the gauge of four feet eight and one-half inches from a point on the boundary between the province of Quebec and Labrador, west of Cape St. Charles.
We hold that the whole of the territory covered by the Bill is in the province of Quebec and therefore within the Dominion. The Bill would seem to assume that it is between Quebec and Labrador as part of Newfoundland.

Explain.

This Bill is intended practically to save the life of this insurance company and to put it on a basis on which it can continue to do insurance business. At the present time I understand the company has not the required reserve; and unless it gets legislation that will enable it to increase its rates, I understand the insurance department intend to discontinue the granting of a license to it. This legislation is similar to that obtained last session by the Imperial Order of Foresters. The Bill will be fully discussed in committee.

I have had numerous letters from secretaries and presidents of the local divisions of the Catholic Mutual Benefit Association in my constituency, objecting to an increase of premiums for the old members of the institution. I presume that the Bill will be discussed in committee, but I wish to bring the attention of the promoter to the fact that it is meeting with very great opposition amongst the old members in my part of the country. If the Department of Finance thinks it is necessary for the life of this institution to increase the premiums on those who became members previous to 1907, it will be necessary, of course, to do so, but I wish to put on record the protests I have received from various divisions of the Catholic Mutual Benefit Association in my constituency of South Cape Breton and in other parts of Nova Scotia.

When the committee
rose at six o'clock I was presenting the case of certain seamen to the minister. I am aware that it is tedious to be taking up the time of the committee; but it seems to be a responsibility that I must discharge, because these poor men, who cannot come here themselves, have placed their case in my hands, and I have no other place to go with it than to the minister. After I have presented the facts to the minister, the responsibility is his and not mine. If these men are not paid, that will be for the minister and the department; but if I do not put the facts before the minister, it will be my responsibility so far as these men are concerned.
Shortly before six o'clock I was pointing out to'the minister that the decisions which these men obtained in the court at North Sydney were set aside on a certiorari by one of the judges of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia on a technicality, namely, that these men, while they were in the service of the Government on this dredge, came within the provisions of chapter 111 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. Section 3 of this chapter reads as follows:
Every vessel employed by the Government of Canada, either temporarily or permanently, shall be deemed to belong-, while so employed, to the Government of Canada for the purposes of this Act.
This vessel, the Port Nelson, was not, I believe, the property of the Government, but at the time these men were aboard her she was temporarily in the service of the Government and for the purposes under discussion was the same as a government-owned vessel. The next section says:
The master of every vessel belonging to the Government of Canada shall cause every person engaged for service in such vessel, after having had this Act read to him, and before he enters upon the discharge of any duty on board of such vessel, to sign his name in the

proper column of a book to be kept by the master for that purpose.
That book, under this statute, takes the place of the articles. These men were not signed under the provisions of chapter 111, but under ordinary seamen's articles of which I have a copy and which are referred to under chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes, the Shipping Act. When a difficulty arose about the wages of these men, of course they proceeded in the courts under the provisions of chapter 113. Now, if these men had been hired under chapter 111, the Government might well say that the men had no recourse against the Government in the courts. But the Government themselves having waived the provision of chapter 111 and having entered into agreement with the men under chapter 113, I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, the men must have their remedy under the law under which they were hired, and it was not open to the Government to deny them that right. It is a well-known principle of law which should be binding between the Government and another party that you cannot approbrate and reprobate-that is, you cannot accept that part of the agreement which suits you and deny the part which provides a remedy against it. It was under these conditions that these men had to support their rights in a court of law. There are four affidavits here, all pretty much the same. I am obliged to read two of them.
Put them on ' Hansard.
I am not permitted to do that under the rules of the House, except by common consent. If it is agreed to, I will certainly-
I think the House will consent.

I have certainly no
desire to take up time in reading them. If they are not put on ' Hansard,' if the minister will read them, my purpose' will be accomplished.
I shall be glad to read them, but I have no doubt they will be put on ' Hansard' with the consent of the House.

Then, I shall be glad to hand these affidavits in. (Affidavits filed with the Clerk of the He use). One thing I wish to point out to the minister. It may Ibe said: Why did these .men go to the courts? Well, of all people on earth, the Government should be bound by the laws enacted by Parliament. Seamen are told by the laws of this country that they must go
a certain way to collect wages that are denied them. Section 187 of the Shipping Act shows that way, and section 188 contains a provision which I particularly wish the minister to note:
Any order for the payment of wages made under the provisions of this section shall be final.
This court, this stipendiary magistrate for the county of Cape Breton, had authority to try that case if these men were engaged under seamen's articles. And that magistrate's decision, under the law, is final. But it was taken by the Government under certiorari, and the court, on a technical point, as I have said, held that the magistrate had no jurisdiction. The principal of estoppel comes in here-and I am speaking in the presence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty)-and should have been invoked on behalf of these men. The Government waived their rights in hiring these men and hired them under seamen's articles, and when the time came for these men to claim their rights under these articles the time was passed when the Government could claim the exemption which in the first place they might have insisted upon. They should have been stopped and the point raised that they could not blow hot and Iblow cold at the same time. The Government are not bound to go into articles, but having gone into them they must stand by what they have done.
I	am glad to shorten the time by not reading these affidavits. I have put the case of these men as completely as I can. One point I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Justice especially, and that is that one of these men is evidently a constituent of his, and so he will understand that while I am presenting this case it should be in abler hands. This Mr. Murphy, who makes the affidavit, says he was, born at Point St. Charles, Montreal, and I understand that that is in the constituency of the Minister of Justice-St. Anne's division. This Mr. Murphy [belongs there; his home is there now. He and these other men were sent to me in North Sydney; I did not go to seek them. As they have come to me, I am bound to take their case as far as I can.

What did the captain
do?
Mr. McKENZIE He refused to pay them, taking shelter under the fact that he was a government employee. He put them in jail and cleared out for the North, leaving

them in jail. Then, when he came back, he kept ahide. I do not think it was a very dignified spectacle to see a gentleman representing the Government of the country hiding behind barns and outhouses, keeping away from a few seamen who had a claim against him. There is a Montreal man, Mr. Parent, whose wages are looked for here as well as those of Mr. Murphy. Mr. Parent says:
I belong to Montreal; X was born at Grand Island, below the city of Montreal.
The other gentlemen live in Montreal but are English by birth. I submit that when the acting Minister of Railways goes through the evidence, while he will find some slight contradiction between the men and the captain, he will find that the second agreement written on the back of the articles here carries out everything that the men say as to the agreement that was made in Montreal. Before concluding, I wish to read a letter which I received the other day from one of these men:
Quebec, May 16, 1914.
Dear Sir,-Just a line to tell you that I got in here on the ss. Calgarian Friday. Would be very pleased if you would write and let me know how you got on with the case. I cannot tell you where the other three are because I have not heard from them for four months. I will he pleased to hear from you next week. Please write me care of secretary of Catholic Seamen's Club.
I remain.
(Sgd) Daniel Murphy.
That is the same Daniel Murphy whose affidavit I read, who belongs to St. Anne's division in the city of Montreal and whose people must be well known to those who are familiar with that city. I trust that the case will be considered and that these men will be found out, wherever they are, and their money paid to them.

I shall he very glad indeed to look into this matter; in fact I shall see that the affidavits and the remarks made by the hon. member are placed before the Minister of Railways himself, who will look into the matter thoroughly. I made a little inquiry into this matter on hearing from the hon. member with reference to it. My information was something to the effect that these men whom they arrived at Sydney were paid off and they did get in some trouble with the captain and were arrested. They were released and I think sailed on another steamer, the Aldershot, within a day or two for England. They did not return to Montreal. I have a letteT of ex-

planation with reference to this matter from Mr. Bonham, of Montreal, who engaged these men. With reference to the suit that was taken by these men in which the hon. member acted for the men, as I understand it was -taken without the knowledge of the Department of Railways and Canals. It is -a well understood fact that in all oases against the Government a fiat must first be obtained from the Government or some notice given to the Crown.
'Mr. McKENZIE: We had no knowledge until the trial that the Government was in this at all; these are the ordinary seamen's articles between the captain and his men.

As soon as the suit was over and it came before the department, the deputy minister, Mr. Campbell, telephoned to Mr. P. C. Bonham of Montreal, and his letter in reply reads as follows:
Montreal, Canada, Sept. 15, 1913. Mr. A. W. Campbell,
Deputy Minister, Railways and Canals, Ottawa, Ont.
Re dredge Port Nelson.
Dear Sir,-Referring to your telephone conversation of Saturday, and replying to your request re conditions on which crew were engaged on dredge Port Nelson from Montreal to Sydney.
Crew were signed on by customs officer for trip from Montreal to Sydney with no reference in articles being made for return fare to Montreal and upon arrival at Sydney crew were mustered on deck and introduced to Captain Saunders who was then taking charge. Crew were then asked how many were willing to proceed to Port Nelson, as before leaving Montreal we made verbal agreement with crew that if Captain Saunders did not have crew at Sydney and he was satisfied with crew I had shipped they would he given an opportunity to proceed to Port Nelson, and upon being asked by Captain Saunders, all hut three volunteered to complete voyage and Captain Saunders framed up a new agreement allowing men the same rate of wages as paid from Montreal to Sydney with return fare from Port Nelson, and under full pay until arrival at port of shipping. All crew willing to proceed then signed articles as per new agreement. Crew then asked for advance of wages from Montreal to Sydney and on the afternoon of September 2 we advanced men from $2 to $10 each, men claiming they required this money to provide themselves with necessary outfit to complete voyage. On the morning of September 3, it was found that a number of crew were not in condition to go to work and Captain Saunders then came to the conclusion that men were not a fit crew and he requested me to pay all crew up to date of September 4, which I did and at same time had all crew sign off on articles, which we consider released owners of any further responsibility on part of crew. All crew signed off in presence of Captain Jones, and at time of signing not one man made any statement or asked for return fare to Montreal, and we

were surprised to learn just before leaving Sydney that some of crew had placed the matter in the hands of attorney, asking for wages and fare and we cannot understand why judgment should be given after crew signed off on articles as they did on September 4.
We left articles in possession of Captain Saunders and we presume same are still on dredge. When hiring crew at Montreal we made verbal agreement with two men for their return fare to Montreal, but same did not appear on articles, but fare was paid them at Sydney for their return passage.
Trusting this will be satisfactory.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd P. C. Bonham.
That is the only information we have in the department. However, I have given instructions to the deputy minister to go carefully into this whole matter and try to get at the bottom of the whole
9	p.m. case in order that the Minister of Railways and Canals may look further into it and come to a conclusion as to what should be done..

I am awfully sorry, but I could not get the information. The chairman of the commission is away from the city and it was late so that I could not get the correspondence. Of course I shall not ask to have the item passed, if the hon. member wishes it to stand, until I get the information asked for.

The members of the
House who are particularly interested in the Railway Estimates made a point of being present to-night and certainly until shortly before six o'clock it was clearly understood that the Railway Estimates would be continued.
I do not wish it to appear that I am not anxious to go on with them.

The hon. gentleman
says it was understood that the Estimates

Mr. BOIV1N: Probably it was understood on the other side of the House.

I wish to bring up a matter of great importance to the constituency of Northumberland, and that is what the Government is doing in regard to removing the rails from that portion of the Intercolonial from Chatham Junction to Blackville. My hon. friend will know what I refer to. The matter was discussed in this House about a year ago, and we found that they had actually started in to move the rails when there was a hitch of some kind. It is a cruel thing to take a railway away from 1,400 people. It means that they will be practically deprived of their means of livelihood. I have a letter here from a Mr. Coughlan-I do not know him-who tells me that the people along the line of railway will simply have to abandon their farms and make a living in some other part of the world. The road has been there for 30 or 40 years, and industries and the business of the country have grown up around it, and now this department is actually taking up the rails and depriving those people of their means of transportation.
I think what the hon. gentleman refers to is a line of railway about 20 miles long, if I remember correctly.
From Chatham Junction to Blackville, in the county of Northumberland.

Two branches of the Intercolonial run parallel to each other on different sides of the river at that place. The bridges on the railway my hon. friend has referred to became dilapidated, and, rather than spend the large amount that would have been necessary to repair them, the Minister of Railways decided to take up the rails on a portion of the road, as there was no necessity for two railways running alongside each other. Bridges are now being built across the river, or it is intended to build them; so the people on both sides of the river will have railway facilities for the whole distance. The rails have not been taken up in the more settled portion of the district. I do not know what the intention of the minister is. The hon. member for Northumberland, who was down there lately, probably knows the situation better than I do.

This matter was brought
up in the House last year, and on that occasion the Minister of Railways said that he had not decided to remove the rails and that nothing would toe done in that regard before the matter had been given the very fullest consideration. Very shortly afterwards the minister went over that line and decided, as I understand it, to go on with the removal of the rails. Last year I protested on behalf of the people who live along that portion of the road from which it is proposed to remove the rails and for this reason: That portion of the road had received aid from the local Government, and the people along that line had enjoyed transportation facilities for some forty years. While it is true that the local traffic was not very large, there were some considerable lumbering interests in that district and there was also a mill near the line of railway. Last year, I drew the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that the Hon. John P. Burchdll, of Nelson, owned a large tract of land there, and wished to cut the timber in proximity to the line so that he could haul the manufactured article to a shipping point.

Is it not true that there is
only one mill on that railway and that the rails still go up to that mill? If there is anything to bring and the railway can fetch it.

I think that is true
enough, but that cannot toe done if the rails are taken up as I understand they are going to be.
I think the hon. gentleman is only imagining trouble. It is time enough to complain when the rails are taken up.

I am not imagining
trouble. Will the minister say that the rails between Chatham Junction and what is known as the Maloney mill will not be taken up?
Is it not true that that mill manufactures only for local purposes, and that it does not ship probably more than one car a month?
That is not correct. They ship a great many carloads, and last year nearly all their business was done in Ontario and Quebec markets.

Do they ship it over this
road?

To a great extent. It is true the Intercolonial railway did run in an engine to bring those cars out, but the dis-

tance is about five or eight miles and it could hardly toe expected that they would keep eight miles of track in repair to draw the product of one saw-mill. The Hon. John P. Burchill through myself, pleaded with the minister not to take up the rails between Blackville and the timber limits I have referred to, because of his interests in the way of timber limits in that locality. The timber is hardwood which, as the minister knows, is difficult to float to a point where it can be sawn into boards. But it is not altogether on that point that I wish to protest. The point I wish to make is that 140 families who have enjoyed for some forty years the privilege of a railroad constructed to some extent toy the public moneys of the country, are to be deprived of their means of transportation. The Government have bought the road at a low price and say that there is no necessity of operating lines on both sides of the river. Is it fair to the people who live on the other side of the river, and who have had these railway services for the last thirty or forty years? The minister talks of the possibility of connecting the other side of the river by bridges. That was mentioned last year, and the minister told us that it was the part of the local government to provide bridges to connect with the railway on the north side of the river. That is absolutely true, but if rails are to be taken up I do ask the minister to make provision for a bridge to connect the two sides of the river. People living along that river are practically without any facilities. The bridge over the Barnaiby river was carried away about one year ago. This bridge over the Barnaby river, that the local government are supposed to keep in repair, has not yet -been rebuilt. There was also a bridge some five or six miles down the river, but that, too, has gone.	It is impossible foT the residents on the south .side of the river to maintain communication, except by canoes, with the other side of the river where the railway is being operated. I protest in the name of the people who have enjoyed these privileges for thirty or forty years. I ask the minister again to reconsider the matter and see if anything can be done to meet the views of the people. I am sure the minister has had this matter presented to him in a strongly and numerously signed petition. The case is quite familiar to the minister, if not to the acting minister, and I know it is to the deputy minister.
Are they all Grits on that side of the river?

I would expect that they would be all Grits next time if the rails are removed. There is a section through which that railway runs which cannot get any railway privileges because it is east of Chatham Junction and away from the river altogether. The people in that location, known as Reynolds, will have no railway facilities whatever. Quite large quantities of pulpwood are shipped from this region to the pulp mills that are located on the opposite side of the river. The people have a grievance, and they will resent very keenly when the opportunity is given them the removal of the rails that they have had the privilege of using for so many years. The minister ought not to go on with this matter without giving it his fullest consideration. I can do no more than draw his attention to it, and once more I protest in the name of the people living between Nelson and Blackville numbering about one hundred families.

The matter did come up last fall, but I do not think anything has been done of late. I do not know what condition the question is in at the present moment. I will bring it, together with the remarks which my hon. friend has made, to the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals. He knows about the matter much better than I do, and I will ask him to give it further consideration.
Do I understand that the acting Minister of Railways and Canals does not intend to proceed further with his Estimates?

I would like to let my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) go on this evening if it is agreeable to hon. gentlemen, because my hon. friend told me that he had arranged that he was to go on with his Estimates. I did not know it myself when I mentioned it this afternoon.

I am in the position of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley); I declined an engagement this evening in OTder to be here and I think there is every reason why the Minister of Railways and Canals should proceed with his Estimates instead of the Estimates of the Justice Department. The latter Estimates are not as a rule contentious, they are largely statutory and I do not think will engage a great deal of time. In view of the fact that we are approaching the conclusion of the session.
and having in mind the relative importance of the Estimates of these two departments, I think that the Minister of Railways and Canals should remain in Supply.

speechtext: I desire to ask the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals if he has any further information to give me witn respect to the report that surveys are being made on a line between St. Peters and Sydney. The minister said yesterday that he was not aware that surveying was being done in that part of the country with a view to building a branch of the Intercolonial in that direction -but that he would give the information later on.
I have to get the information from Moncton and I have not received it ye-t. I do not know whether these surveys are being made by the Intercolonial; they are not surveys by the department.

This is not along the line of the Intercolonial railway at all. There is a line of railway owned by the Cape Breton Railway Company operating between St. Peters and Point Tuppei. It is reported that negotiations are going on between the company and the Government with a view to purchasing that railway and, furthermore, that a corps of engineers is at present engaged by the department working on the location of a line of railway between St. Peters and Sydney. That is altogether separate from the Intercolonial.

That is a matter with reference to the revision of the grade. The deputy minister tells me that he sent the .question of the hon. gentleman to Moncton to get the information -but he has not yet got a Teply. I will have the information for the hon. gentleman before we get through the Estimates.

I have been asking these
questions several days, and no information is forthcoming. I repeat that this survey, which it is said is being made, has nothing

to do with the Intercolonial. If they are making a survey it must be with the view of building a line from St. Peter's to Syd-k ney.

No independent survey has been authorized' by me since the 1st of February last, when I became acting minister. If there is any such survey it must be authorized by Moncton, and I will have to get the information from Moncton.
Would the management of the Intercolonial undertake to survey for a new line without instructions from Ottawa?
The Intercolonial railway has several parties out, and they may be surveying to get different grades or for the purpose of constructing a piece of road in tne interest of the Intercolonial.
That is what the hon. member (Mr. Kyte) wants to. know.
A letter has been sent to Moncton giving the full question of the hon. member, and we will get the information in good time.
Why not send a message by wire.
Surely the hon. member can wait for a few days.

I have for several days been calling attention to this matter. The newspapers state day after day that the Intercolonial railway has undertaken to survey for a railway line in that part of my constituency, and I shall be pleased indeed to know that the Government has at last undertaken to build that extension of the Intercolonial.
The hon. gentleman has answered his question: he says the newspapers state that the Intercolonial railway is making surveys in his county with a view to extend the Intercolonial.
I want to know from the minister if that is correct.

If a survey party is there the management of the Intercolonial is no doubt looking over the routs; the hon. gentleman himself admits that.
Mr. KYTE.; I said that the Conservative newspapers, which are not very reliable, are reiterating the statement that Government engineers are surveying for this line of railway, and I ask the minister if he has given instructions for any such survey?
I have not given instructions, and neither has the deputy minister. I have inquired from Moncton.
Will the minister be able to tell me to-morrow?
I will get the information as soon as I can.
You can get the information by eleven o'clock to-morrow morning.
I will do the best I can.
I wish now to ask the minister if the department has completed arrangements for the prosecution of the work on the St. Peter's canal?

Tenders were called for the construction of a new lock at St. Peter's, and Mr. Weller was the lowest tenderer, and the work was to be done on schedule prices. When the work had been proceeded with for some time, it was found that the material was different from that specified, and the contractor could not go on with the work at the prices without incurring hearvy loss.- In addition, it was thought that where the lock was to be constructed was of rock formation, but that was a mistake, and the chief engineer has recommended that the lock be built further down, which would necessitate the closing of the canal for one season if the work is undertaken now. The chief engineer tells me he would have to increase the price in the original contract of 39o. a yard to about 79 cents for removing the material and from $5,000 to $89,000 for unwiatering, which means altogether an extra expenditure of $100,000 if Mr. Weller is allowed to continue the work at the prices recommended by the chief engineer, Mr. Bowden. Even with $100,000 added to the original con templated cost, Mr. Weller's tender would be less than the lowest tender for the original lock. I personally feel that Mr. Weller should be allowed to proceed with the work, as recommended by Chief Engineer Bowden, but I left the matter over until I could discuss it with Mr. Cochrane, and Mr. Cochrane, having taken the advice of Mr. Bowden, I think he also is of the same opinion. I feel like submitting the matter to Council on Mr. Bowden's recommendation to give the work to Mr. Weller at the increased prices. We will then have the lock on a good foundation, and, according to Mr. Bowden, it would be a much better job in the end. 1 am giving the hon. member all the in-

formation I have. He knows the situation there, and I would like to have his views as to whether or not he would agree with Mr. Bowden's report that it would be well to construct the lock at the place where Mr. Bowden has suggested; to give the work to Mr. Weller and to proceed at once. If we have to advertise again for tenders, we must have a new specification, and it will take probably six weeks for advertising and six or eight weeks before we can get started with the work. Mr. Bowden claims that, unless we can start with the work with Mr. Weller who has the plant on the ground, we shall not be able to complete it without closing the canal for two years. If we start now, we shall only have to close the canal during this season.

As the hon. minister has
intimated, I am quite familiar with the conditions that exist with respect to the improvement on the St. Peter's canal, and I shall be perfectly willing to accept any recommendation made by Mr. Bowden, the chief engineer of the Department of Railways. I am sure he would not make any recommendation with respect to the carrying out of this work that involves an increase on the original amount intended to be paid for it unless he had good ground for making such a report.
The situation is somewnat pressing there at the present moment. As I stated on another occasion, when I discussed this matter, the condition of unemployment in that part of the country is very serious at the present time. A great many people were employed during the past season on the construction work on the St. Peter's canal, and they were depending on that source of employment for the present year. Up to the present time, however, no action has been taken, and there is a great deal of disappointment on the part of the labourers in the community in respect of the postponement of the resumption of operations on this canal. I have nothing to say as to whether or not it would be preferable to call for new tenders now or to award the contract to Mr. Weller; but I am bound to say that, in view of the delay which will be occasioned by calling for new tenders, it seems desirable that a new contract, be entered into at the earliest possible moment. Whatever recommendation Mr. Bowden makes with regard to this matter, if in his judgment the work, in view of the change in the plans, will involve an additional expenditure of $100,000, I am sure it will
be accepted by the public generally as being the best that can be done under the circumstances. I would therefore urge strongly that the minister will without any unnecessary delay insure the early resumption of the work on the St. Peter's canal by making a new contract according to the recommendation of the chief engineer of the department.
I promise the hon. member that I will try, if possible, to bring the matter before Council to-morrow.

While this canal is not in my constituency, I think I am perhaps more interested in the completion of the canal than the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), because a great deal of the traffic that passes through it comes from my constituency. I am perfectly in accord with what the hon. member has said as to what should be done in giving the contract to the present contractor. Certainly the minister should put the very best man he can find in charge of the work, and see that it does not drag along in the snail-crawl, death-like style in which it has been carried forward since this gentleman has had the contract, but that some life and snap is put into it and that it is finished within a reasonable time.

I would like to ask the minister for information in regard to the proposed branch railway in my constituency. He assured the House on several occasions that the matter was receiving consideration; and a few weeks ago, my hon. friend the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) placed a resolution before the House asserting that the time had arrived when the branch railways should be built in those parts of the Maritime provinces that are now without railway accommodation. This resolution had direct reference to the Guysborough railway. Somewhat to the surprise of my hon. friend, that resolution was accepted by the Government and was passed by the House. When the House of Commons say that the time has arrived to take action on a matter, then the time has arrived; and I was very much surprised, on looking over the Supplementary Estimates yesterday, to find that no provision had been made for these branch lines that were discontinued and cancelled by the present Government when they came into power. If it is not the policy of the Government to do anything in the matter of the proposed Guysborough railway the

minister should frankly say so; and if he ha3 any information to give to the House, I would like to 'have it now.

Do I understand the hon.
member to say that this is for taking over a line or for building a new line through his constituency?

I am referring to the proposed new branch line from Sunnybrae to Guysborough, which was contracted for * by the late Government in 1911, on which the money was voted, the contract made and a part of the line purchased from the Nova Scotia Steel Company, and $100,000 spent. When, this Administration came into power they cancelled the contract, abandoned the road, and have ever since that day been throwing out hints that they intend to do something and that the matter is under consideration. The resolution moved by my hon. friend the member for North Cape Breton referred to the Guysborough branch along with a branch in his own constituency. The House accepted that resolution, and said that the time had arrived to deal with the matter. I trust that the minister has not overlooked these circumstances, and that he understands now what I am endeavouring to place before him. I want to know what the policy of the Government is i:n, regard to this matter, whether they Teally intend to do anything in the way of constructing these branch lines or not.

The hon. member will remember that the Minister of Railways came to this House with a policy of branch lines in the lower provinces, and unfortunately the Senate threw it out >and he was not able to take any action in so far as the branch lines were concerned.
This has nothing to do with that question at all. You have already secured the branch line that was required; you have a deed of it and you require no aid from the Senate in that matter.

This was the building of a new line. No work had been done, and the contract was cancelled. The hon. member knows that the Minister of Railways and Canals has not taken any further action yet. I do not know what he has in mind; but he prepared the Estimates, and they have been brought down, and he will not oe able to proceeed with the work this year. He, no doubt, has in mind to consider the

taking over of other lines in the lower provinces as soon as he can do so, but he has not been able to do so during the present session.
It will be done before the next election.

A railroad in the hon. minister's mind is not much good to us in the county of Guysborough. The minister informed the House during the present session that there was a survey being made of this proposed line. Can he tell us if he has any report from his engineers as to what they have done?

We have no report with reference to what has been done. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) made the remark that this would probably be done just before the next election. If *1 remember aright, this line was surveyed just before the last election, and the contract let. I promise the hon. member that we shall not use this line for any political campaign such as was done at the last election. I do not think this Government would be guilty of doing anything of that kind. We will start a long time before an election or immediately after.

I think I shall have to correct my hon. friend with regard to that matter. The branch line policy of the late Government was only adopted about the session of 1910. Immediately afterwards, a survey was made of the proposed Guysborough branch, and at the commencement of the session of 1911 provision was made for going forward with this branch line. No one at that date anticipated an election. Parliament was in its third year. The reciprocity agreement had not been laid before the House, and everybody expected that Parliament would last at least four years, and perhaps five. Under these circumstances, before there was any intention of having an election, $1,000,000 was placed in the Estimates and voted by Parliament. The branch line from Sunnybrae to Ferrona was purchased from the Nova Scotia Steel Company, and the department paid the company $100,000 for it, and took it over. Tenders were called for and received; the engineers decided on the tenders, and the contract was let. The circumstances were similar in regard to the branch line in the county of Halifax which at that time was represented by two Conservatives. Both lines were in exactly the same position- contracts had been let, and in each case $1,000,000 was voted. The late Government

was broad enough to deal with the question in a proper and business-like manner. They did not regard the fact that one county was represented by Conservatives and the other by a Liberal, but undertook the building of these lines merely with a view to the traffic requirements of the country. But the present Government was not broad enough to carry out that policy, but because the county I represent sent me, a supporter of the Opposition, to Parliament, the Government cancelled the line in Guysborough and continued the line in Halifax. I know that my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden), is a little ashamed of the action of his Government in regard to that matter and does not want it referred to very often. It is not very creditable to his Government, and it is hard to believe that the Prime Minister of a great country like Canada would not be broad enough to see across the line fence of the county he represents. I hope the Government will make an effort to redeem its reputation before the present Parliament expires. I have kept the matter 'before them constantly, as it was my duty to do, in hopes of inducing them to do something with regard to it. But the acting minister says he does not know the policy or intentions of the Minister of Railways in this matter. If he will be kind enough to find find out what the hon. gentleman's intentions are I shall be very much obliged, and when his Estimates come up again, perhaps he will give us some information as to whether the Government really intend to take action in regard to this matter or not.

When some of the other
Intercolonial Estimates are on, I will have more information. I cannot give the hon. gentleman further information to-night.
Could not the minister proceed with the railway Estimates for Prince Edward Island now? There are only a few items, and there are some matters I wish to discuss.
We are on the Hudson Bay railway now. But if hon. members will carry this item, I shall be glad to take up the Prince Edward Island Taiiway Estimates.
On account of the illness of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Richards), I am the only Liberal Prince Edward Island member here and cannot be present all the time, and I wish to go on to-night.
There will be other items.

But I might not be here when they are brought up. I am sure that the hon. members from other provinces will be willing to take up these items now.
Prince Edward Island railway

to increase accommodation and facilities along the line, $5,200.

Last year when we were discussing the Estimates the Minister of Railways told me that he had received a petition from the inhabitants of Bridget-town and Dundas asking him to build a short piece of railway connecting these settlements with the main line either at Cardigan, St. Peter's or Souris. He told me he would have a survey and report made during the summer. The survey I know was not made, and I suppose the report was not made either. Could the minister tell us the reason?

As the hon. member states,
there has been no survey or report. I could not give him any particular reason except that the survey parties for the Intercolonial were busy on the mainland. Also, it was not possible to proceed with construction on the Prince Edward Island railway at the points mentioned by the hon. member last year, and so a survey did not seem necessary. Surveys can be made, of course, when we are ready to proceed with the work. There is an item in the Estimates to pay for survey parties along the Intercolonial, and we could send one of these parties to Prince Edward Island and pay for it out of this fund. But until money is voted to build the railway it is hardly necessary to send a survey party.

I understood that the
course is for the minister to have a survey made before he proceeds so far as to put an item in the Estimates. He wants to know what the whole cost will be. There was $100,000 last year for surveys and reports generally, and it was out of that appropriation, the minister told me, this work would be paid for.
I said it could be done.

Will the minister say
that he will have the work done this summer?

I will take the matter up
with the Minister of Railways and Canals, and if he feels that he is justified in asking next session for a vote to proceed with the work, the survey party will be sent.
Have not you the same item this year?

The item for survey parties
-yes.
Well, will the minister have it this year?
We will have it this year if we can spare the party from the work they are on.

A few days ago the minister received a petition from Hetherdale, Montague Head and Montague and other settlements to extend the Montague branch to connect with the main line. The minister said he would look into the matter. Will he have that survey made this year?
I will try to have that survey made too.

I will make inquiries tomorrow and take it up with the minister.
Prince Edward Island railway-to provide car ferry, construct terminals and necessary connections, $1,500,000.
The minister told me last year that the car ferry would be in operation this year. What progress has been made and when does he expect the ferry to be in operation?

I understand that the car
ferry will be ready at the time stated, that is, early in the fall of 1915. The deputy minister informs me that owing to a strike on the other side there may be a delay of a month in completing the boat. That would make it the end of September or the first of October.
When does the minister expect to have the piers ready?
In time for the ferry.
Is there any show of having the whole thing going before the next election?

Oh, yes, we will have the whole thing going before the election.

It is my desire to make my remarks as brief as is consistent with a proper presentation of facts which I think should be placed before this House. Before entering into a discussion of the Penitentiary Commission, I wish to make a few general remarks leading up to that. I live about three miles from the village of Portsmouth, where Kingston penitentiary is situated. In consequence of my nearness to that village and that institution hon. gentlemen will understand that it is only natural that I should hear from time to time of the doings in that penitentiary. After the change of Government in 1911, complaints were made to me by guards and ex-guards of that institution and to those

complaints were added specific charges made by a gentleman who had occupied several positions in that institution, covering a period of something like twenty years. I refer to Major Hughes, who at the time of the change of Government was accountant at the penitentiary and who has since that time been appointed one of the inspectors of penitentiaries. I felt that these charges coming from such a source from an official holding the position which he held and corroborated by
10	p.m. other officials, were of such a nature that I should lay them before the Minister of Justice. I did so verbally and later on, I think about nine months before the commission was appointed, I placed my charges before the minister in writing. I may say that on the night of March 29 or the morning of March 30, a convict by the name of Chartrand effected a partial escape from the prison and the night watchman, a man named Smith, was suspended on the first of April, in connection with that attempted escape. Smith came to me on the day of his suspension and complained that he did not think he was getting a fair deal, that the day guard on that particular part of the prison was more responsible for the escape than he and was still on duty. I wrote to the department and asked for an investigation, and on the 4th of April McConville, the day guard, was suspended.
The minister appointed Mr. Hackett, then his private secretary, I believe, to make an investigation into that escape. I subsequently wrote to the department asking for a copy of the report in regard to that investigation. On the 3rd September, 1912, I received a letter from Mr. Hackett, which 1 will not take up the time of the House in reading but the substance of which was that he had not had time to make a detailed report, but that in course of time he would do so and send me a copy. That summer I went out West, and coming back after some weeks I made a second request and was informed that Mr. Hackett had only made a verbal report. On the 2nd of December, 1912, I sent the following letter to the Minister of Justice, which I want to place on ' Hansard ' because it is intimately connected with what I shall have to say later.
Hon. C. J. Doherty, M.P.,
Minister of Justice.
My dear Sir,-I beg to request your serious consideration of the following charges which in my opinion warrant my asking for the removal from office of Deputy Warden O'Leary and Dr.
Phelan, surgeon of Portsmouth penitentiary. I charge Deputy Warden O'Leary:
(a)	With petty and persistent persecution of guards and keepers;
(b)	With political partisanship ;
(c)	With testifying falsely at investigation held at the prison;
(d)	With consorting with ex-convicts;
(e)	With gross neglect of his duty resulting in attempts to escape;
I charge the surgeon, Dr. Phelan:
(a)	With gross political partisanship;
(b)	With using violent and indecent language to a guard in the presence of others;
(c)	With conniving at the absence of a guard at an election trial where said guard was wanted as a material witness;
(d)	With grafting, by asking for and receiving money from guards, to which he had no just or honest claim, etc.
There are other officials whose conduct should be inquired into.
If you would prefer it I will make these charges on the floor of the House and ask for the appointment of a Eoyal Commission of Inquiry.
Trusting that the foregoing will receive your early attention.
I remain, yours sincerely,
J. W. Edwards.
On December 4, the Minister of Justice in acknowledging my letter asked if I would be willing that the charges should be placed before the gentlemen I had accused. I answered him verbally that I thought that was only proper and right, but that I would prefer that the charges should be placed in the hands of those gentlemen when the commission was appointed; and when the commission was appointed that was done. On the 25th August, 1913, eighteen months after I had verbally made my charges to the minister and nine months after I had made them in writing, an Order in Council was passed appointing George Milnes Macdonnell, K.C., Frederick Etherington, M.D., both of Kingston, and Joseph Patrick Downey of Orillia as a Royal Commission under the Inquiries Act to investigate and report. I am mentioning the time which intervened between my verbally making the charges and the appointment of the commission not in any censorious spirit. I recognize that at the time I made my charges verbally the Government had only been in power a very short time, and I appreciate that the Minister of Justice like the head of every other department had a great deal to occupy his time and attention. I find no fault in that respect.
Without making any detailed comment at present on the personnel of the commission, I want to say that it is open to objection on the ground that Mr. Downey, who holds a position under the Ontario Government, was appointed as one of the

44g<5

commissioners. I also question the wisdom ol appointing to that commission two gentlemen from the city of Kingston. Of course, I am only expressing my own view, and, in fairness to the Justice Department, I may say that at the time the names of the commissioners were first mentioned as appointees, I saw no reason why they should not perform their duties properly and well. But I think I will show before I get through that they did not fulfil their duties properly, and that from the very outset they prevented evidence from coming out which ought to have come out, and that the report which has been laid bn the table of this House is, so far as the charges I made are concerned,a mass of misrepresentation. I will go farther and say that their report, in so far as it deals with the charges 1 made, contains more misrepresentations to the square inch than any document ever tabled in this House since there was a parliament of Canada.
I might read the terms of the commission, which are as follows:
(a)	The state and management of the Kingston penitentiary;
(b)	The conduct of the officers and employees of said penitentiary, so far as the same relates to their official duties, and
(c)	Generally, the subject of the conduct and administration of penitentiaries, including such methods as may conduce to the permanent reformation of the convicts, and, without prejudice to the punishment which convicts should properly undergo and without undue burden upon the public funds, tend to mitigate as far as may be found possible the sufferings entailed by their confinement upon those dependent upon them.
I wish to draw particular attention to the following paragraph:
Provided that the inquiries under paragraphs (a) and (b) shall not extend hack over a longer period than five years, except in so far as the commissioners may deem it desirable, in the public interest, to inquire into any particular matter or matters antecedent to such period.
In regard to the five-year limit, which I may say was repeatedly invoked by the commissioners to 'shut out evidence in respect to the charges I had made, I recognize that it may have been, and no doubt was, put in by the Minister of Justice without any intention of shutting out evidence in respect of the charges I had made. I took the ground at the first meeting of the commission that the Minister of Justice did not and could not mean that the five-year limit was to apply to the charges I had made. I argued that the minister must have considered an investigation of 
the charges I had made in the public interest, or otherwise he would not have sent those charges to the commission to be investigated; and that if the charges were in the public interest, and if it was in the public interest to investigate those charges-and the best evidence of that was the sending of those charges to the commissioners-I could not conceive of placing a limitation upon the commission which would preclude and prevent an investigation of the charges they were asked to investigate. That was the line of argument I took before the commission. I believe the commissioners misunderstood the five-year limitation as contained in the terms of the commission. At all events, I am convinced that they made a misuse of that limitation, and excluded evidence which it was in the interests of this House to have, in order that it might he in a position to properly estimate the men whose conduct was called in question. I had taken some responsibility as a member of this House in making charges against the deputy warden, the surgeon and Mr. Wilson, the hospital overseer, but in making these charges I had no personal animus against any of these men. I did not know the deputy warden to see him until after I had made the charges when he was pointed out to me on the street. I had never had more than half a dozen conversations with Dr. Phelan in my life and my acquaintance with Mr. Wilson was very slight. Mr. Wilson had been appointed by this Government. I made the charges against these men regardless of their creed or politics because I believed their conduct should be investigated and because I thought it was in the public interest that the fullest inquiry should be made into the manner in which that institution was being run. I have no person to nominate for any of these positions if they were to be vacated tomorrow. In view of the fact that I have preferred charges against these men I would not think of suggesting any persons to take their places.
The effect of the five-year limitation, in the way in which the commissioners looked at it, was to exclude a great deal of evidence which could have been given by the present inspector, Major Hughes, because the time when he was best acquainted with the institution was when he was chief keeper. The fact that he was not allowed to go back beyond five years simply prevented him from giving the evidence which he otherwise would have given and which I think would have been in the interest of

this House to have had presented to it. Before taking up the report itself, I want to read a short extract from an article in the Toronto Globe which was written just after the commission had held a few sittings :
The Kingston Investigation.
All the influences are towards suppression in the Kingston penitentiary investigation. Convicts do not dare reveal unwholesome facts, knowing their own helplessness under the men they may expose. Applicants for pardons tell what the authorities want told and conceal what they want to conceal. Ex-convicts in respectable positions do not want the dark chapters of their lives published. Those who are poor know they may be arrested with impunity on hollow charges at any time, and that they are open to varied persecutions. This makes them fearful of offending the authority they have learned to dread. On the commission, too, there is an obvious desire to suppress and whitewash. But in spite of all these influences enough is leaking out to show that a prison is a prison.
This e'xjtract from .the /Toronto Globe very adequately depicts the situation. I could quote from a number of other papers but I do not think it is necessary to do so. The prisoners wtho might hove given evidence were afraid to do so for fear that thleir chances of getting out on parole would be lessened or for fear that remission of sentence would be lost to them. The guards were in much the same position; they knew that they were largely in the hands of the head officials of the institution who might report them; for trivial offences and make it very uncomfortable for them. Prom the beginning of the investigation that was very manifest. Men who had expressed themselves very openly, pointedly and substantially in regard to the officers against whom my charges were made were very close-mouthed when it came to the matter of the investigation. This statement applies not merely to the guards jmd under officials of the institution. It applies to a certain extent also to a gentleman who was responsible for the principle charges which were made; that is Major Hughes, the present inspector. I do not know whether the larger salary which goes with the position of inspector as compared with that received by the accountant had anything to do with it hut there was something which had an effect upon his stiffness of backbone that is supposed to be very characteristic in some families. I say that because I want to impress upon the House the fact that if you want to consider this report fairly if you want to arrive at a correct conclu-283J
sion, you can only do so by properly estimating the position in which these men were placed. There was a certain amount of intimidation of the officials of the institution as well as of the convicts which had a tendency to prevent evidence from being brought out. When you add to that the fact-<and I will prove that it is a fact-that the commissioners at the very outset showed a disposition to shut out evidence and to act as a whitewashing commission, you will understand that it made the position very difficult and it warrants me in coming to this House and placing some facts before you in order that you may understand the true condition of affairs in connection with this institution.
The commissioners never seemed to realize the position they occupied. They were appointed to investigate and inquire but from the very outset they seemed to regard themselves ias a court trying a certain case. As I understand their position, it was their duty to investigate and inquire, obtain all the evidence possible and lay that evidence before this House. It was up to this House to act as a court and a judge of the evidence, excluding what it did not think was of value, taking into consideration what it did consider to be of value and arriving at a proper conclusion a3 to what should he done to improve the condition of this institution. But the commissioners seemed to regard it as their duty not only to get a certain amount of evidence but to try the case themselves and to sit as judges. I want to point out some very peculiar things that were done by the commission. One of the gentlemen that I made charges against was Mr. Wilson, the hospital overseer who was appointed by this Government. The Penitentiary Commission placed an advertisement in the Kingston papers asking any and every person who had any charges or complaints to make to come forward and present these charges to the commission. That was signed by the three commissioners. That had a very good look on the face of it and the public, reading it said: These men are anxious to get at the facts, they have invited men to come forward and make complaints. I went before the commission and I told them that because of reports that had come to me I felt it my duty to ask them to investigate certain charges against the hospital overseer.
448c

The hospital overseer, I have been told, would not get out of bed at night to attend sick convicts. There is a room provided for the hospital overseer and for hie assistant, which they are supposed to use and take turns about at night, one stays up one night and the other another night for the express purpose of being convenient to the convicts, so that if one of them should become ill he could call upon the hospital overseer or his assistant, who, if they thought it advisable, could call the surgeon out to attend the sick man. It was stated to me by several that the hospital overseer absolutely refused to get up and that in consequence the convicts were obliged to remain in their cells and suffer all night. I thought that was a matter that should be investigated. I am not one who thinks that convicts ought to be treated like people outside of prison; I know the first thing is to punish them for the offence they have committed against society, but I do say that they ought to be regarded as human Ibeings and treated with humanity. Before I get through I think I will be able to show that some of these convicts have been treated worse than any .man in this House would treat his horses, his cattle, or his dogs. I believe that I would have been guilty of neglect of my duty if I did not place that information before the minister, and I also believe that I would not be doing my duty as a representative of the people if I did net place these facts before the House as I understand them. What did Mr. Maodonell, the chairman of the commission, do when I went before him and placed my complaint in writing against Mr. Wilson, and asked him to call three persons to give evidence in regard to the charge? Did Mr. Macdonell say:	Certainly, that is what I have been advertising in the papers for; I shall Ibe glad to do so: Not at all. He did his best to persuade me not to press the charge against Mr. Wilson, and he wanted me to write to Ottawa about it. I said: No, I am not going to write to Ottawa at all; you have been appointed as a commission to investigate these matters, and here is something I think you should investigate. I threw the paper on the table and I said: I expect you to investigate that charge.
iLet me state something further with regard to this Mr. Macdonell. An exguard of the institution, Percy Johnston, a respectable citizen of Kingston, went before the chairman of the commission in answer to his advertisement and preferred a charge 
against the deputy and against the surgeon. What did Mr. Macdonell, the chairman of the commission, do? He had placed this advertisement in the papers asking for persons to come forward with their charges, and Mr. Johnston, a respectable citizen, came before him and presented his charge in writing against these two men, and this chairman of the Royal Commission told Mr. Johnston to go home and keep out of this. I have here the affidavit of Mr. Johnston, which reads:
I Percy Jlohnston of the city of Kingston in the county of Prontenac make oath and say.
1. That I formerly was a guard in the Kingston penitentary.
z. i noticed an advertisement in the Kingston Standard inviting all persons having any knowledge of any complaints or irregularities concerning said penitentiary to bring the same before a commission for investigating said penitentiary.
3. Said advertisement was signed by G. M. Macdonell, K.C., and on the 7th October last I called at Mr. Macdonell's office and presented a complaint to him in writing. I told him the nature of my complaint and that I had been most unjustly used and that I could produce witnesses to testify that I had been put out of my office by fraud and deceit.
Mr. Macdonell told me that this matter did not concern me and that if I would take' his advice I would go home and let the matter drop.
Sworn before me at the city of Kingston in the county of prontenac this 11th October A.D. 1913.
Percy M. Johnson. , Chas. Webster,	.
A commissioner, etc., H.C.J.

Would the hon. member read the commission that was issued to these men? We will then be better able to say whether they were acting outside or inside of their jurisdiction. They would certainly be limited by the authority they got from the Government.

I have already read the commission at the opening of my remarks, and it is to be found on the first page of the printed report. I shall send a copy over to my hon. friend. A man named Chapman, convict on parole, having seen something in the paper about evidence that was given by another person before the commission, wrote a letter to the deputy warden saying that if he were brought up as a witness he could give evidence in favour of the deputy warden.
