testified falsely; but the matter of his testifying falsely was not investigated at the time, and the commission refused to allow any investigation into the matter at the time they held their sittings at Kingston.

Perhaps the hon. member should have read another sentence below the one he read. Mr. Douglas Stewart was asked:
Q. Do I understand that you are responsible for recommending this method of punishment, the hosing?-A. I am responsible for the regulation. I introduced it after consultation with Sir Oliver Mowat, who was not a cruel man, as a substitute for the cat.
It seems that Mr. Douglas Stew-art is responsible for the introduction of the hose, and not the deputy warden.

That does not affect my point in the least. I called attention to the fact that the commissioners in this report say very explicitly that hosing is cruel and inhuman; that they also say that they find no evidence of any cruelty on the part of the deputy warden, Mr. O'Leary, and that the evidence clearly shows that the deputy warden did practise., punishment which the commissioners say is cruel and inhuman.
But if it was the regulation, the deputy warden only carried out his duty.

I am not saying it was not the regulation. I am afraid my hon. friend does not appreciate my point. So far as the regulations are concerned, if he has read the report at all, he will see that the commissioners distinctly call attention to certain of the regulations and say that they should be abolished for the reason that they believe they are cruel and inhuman; but here is one thing that was done, whether it was a regulation or not, by the deputy warden, and the commissioners consider that it was cruel and inhuman to do it. Nevertheless they say they cannot find any evidence of his being guilty of cruelty or inhumanity to the convicts.

It seems a matter of
opinion as to whether it was cruel or inhuman or not.

Another misrepresentation on the part of the commissioners is where they say that Stewart-that is, the counsel appointed by the Government- says that Hughes is the chief witness. That is not correct. The evidence does not say that. The evidence says that Hughes was one of the principal witnesses, but not the chief witness, not the only witness upon 
whom we were depending to substantiate the charges.
I also quote an expression which they credit to Major Hughes, and which is found on page 18:
Major Hughes himself says: ' In my day as chief keeper I did not think the men had an awful lot to complain of in that kind of thing '-
Meaning persecution.

' but latterly there has been a great deal of gossip. I cannot give you that, but the rosters will show.'
That is deliberately intended to deceive the House and the country. Hughes swore before the commission that there was gross discrimination and that when he was chief keeper he had spats and battles with the deputy warden, in endeavouring to prevent discrimination. In part of his evidence he gives specific instances of petty persecution on the part of the deputy warden. The statement that Hughes was represented as saying is a shameless misrepresentation, as conveying a representation which his evidence throughout shows he bad no intention of conveying and did not convey.
Hughes says:
That the deputy warden had an unhappy manner of dealing with the men; that he irritated every man when he went to say anything to him; that he had an intolerable manner of dealing with the men.
He gave specific instances of all these statements.
On page 20 of the report, you will find the names of guards and ex-guards. The report
says:
Of the guards and ex-guards referred to by Major Hughes in his evidence, the following were called, and a summary of their evidence on the charge of petty and persistent persecution of guards is given below.
In the first place, that misrepresents the facts by quoting some words which I used with regard to Major Hughes. Then the commissioners pretend or profess to name twenty-nine guards who were mentioned by Major Hughes in his evidence, when, as a matter of fact, only fourteen out of those twenty-nine were mentioned by him. A reference to the evidence will show that. Why did they do so? Let us take those men and the summary of their evidence as given by the report. The commissioners refer to Smith, for instance, who was one of the men mentioned by Major Hughes. Smith is one of the men mentioned by Major Hughes. They profess to give a summary of his evidence in these words:

Smith complains he was improperly dismissed. Deputy warden not responsible.
As a matter of fact, Smith diid not complain of anything of the kind, nor does the evidence show that he did. Mr. Whiting, who was acting as counsel for the deputy warden .and Dr. Phalen, questioned Smith along these lines as follows:
Q. I suppose you felt a little sore about being dismissed?.-A. No, I did not, I was very glad to get away from night duty.
Now, this is a direct contradiction of this professed summary of the evidence of Smith. I would like to call your attention to some of the things that Smith did complain of, and which they did not mention at all. The report suppresses the fact that Smith did complain of the conduct of the derputy warden. When Smith asked to get off to take his child to the hospital to be operated upon, he was refused. He was reported, though others were not reported, for late winding. They also ignore entirely Smith's sworn statement as to O'Leary having been drinking. These things they leave out of the report, and then profess to give a summary of Smith's evidence in the words I have quoted.
Did not the hon. gentleman himself state that Smith was suspended on April 1, and came to the hon. gentleman and complained?

The hon. gentleman has left out two or three words which make all the difference. Smith came to me on the same day he was suspended, and complained that he was not being given a square deal and was not 'being treated the same as others-that there was another guard more responsible and more to blame than he was, and this guard was left on duty while he, Smith, was suspended. That is what I said, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Chisholm) did not understand. Take another case:
Montgomery complained that his post was not changed as often as others.
That is not a fair summary of his evidence. Montgomery says he resigned his position because he felt he was being ill-treated by the deputy warden, that others were given special holidays which the deputy warden denied to him. He also testified that he smelt liquor on the deputy warden. These things are left out of the report. Then, take McQuade. They affect to summarize his evidence by saying:
I have nothing to say against him.
This refers to the deputy warden. But they suppressed the fact that McQuade swore that the deputy warden called him a damned fool in the presence of another guard and a convict, and O'Leary admits it. This is a direct violation of the regulations. Also he says that the deputy warden put up the convict Connors to trap him, and that the deputy warden refused to let him off to move. He had to get np at two o'clock in the morning, work all day at moving, and came to the penitentiary to go on night duty at 6.30 p.m. That may seem a small thing, but that is exactly where the discrimination and petty persecution came in. This man was refused a reasonable request, while others had such requests granted repeatedly. That is one of the reasons that led to- a great deal of trouble.
In summarizing Aikin's evidence, the report says:
He complains of the deputy warden spying on him.
But the report leaves out the fact that the deputy warden in his manner of speaking in the presence of the guards acted contrary to the regulations. He told Aikins that Inspector Stewart had charged him with lying down on duty, and Inspector Stewart stated that the deputy warden had lied. The deputy warden gets him out of bed at ten o'clock at night to go to the prison to go on duty, and after he gets there he tells him to go home again. He was reprimanded for late winding when helping a sick convict. The convict had been taken sick in the night, had fallen out of his cot and was vomiting on the floor. This guard stopped to attend to the wants of the convict, lifted him up and put him on the bed, and consequently was a few minutes late in winding, for which he was reprimanded by the deputy warden. The deputy warden said:	If he dies you
are not responsible. Yet these commissioners say they can find no evidence of any cruelty or inhumanity on the part of the deputy warden. This is all left out of the report and they present what purports to be a summary of the evidence of this man in the few words I have given. They also leave out his statement that the deputy warden ordered him to stay out on the platform in a driving storm of hail and sleet, though the towers are provided for the express purpose of protecting the guards in time of storm. Many other statements are made which are left out entirely.

They say they summarized the evidence of Davis by the statements that his complaints were childish, yet in his evidence Davis makes some very serious charges against the deputy. The same thing is true in regard to Johnston. I will not take up time with going over all these. But for the evidence of Patterson they present this summary:
He blames the deputy warden for his dismissal but cannot establish it.
But they leave out the fact that Patterson swore that the deputy warden gave false testimony. His statement will be found at page 983. And he asserts that he and others who gave evidence in a former investigation were discharged. In regard to Ingledew, they summarize his evidence in these words:
Kept a note-book; willing witness against the deputy warden; not asked re favouritism.
Now, Ingledew swears that the deputy warden recommended that he should be fined $5 because, having found a box containing some scissors and other things like that in the ward back of one of the cells, he took it to the head office. The deputy warden complained about his doing it, but if he 'had not taken it to the head office the charge would have been made against him of neglect of duty. He did what he conceived to be his duty, and the deputy warden recommended that he should be fined $5 for it. In regard to Bannister, they say that they summarize his evidence in these words:
Complained of being reprimanded before guards and convicts.
Let us see if that is a fair summary of Bannister's evidence. On March 15, 1911, Bannister was working in the deputy warden's house. He was sent down to a wharf to take charge of a gang of convicts when the thermometer was ten below zero. He asked for the usual shanty protection which is given guards having charge of men outside. This was refused him by the deputy warden. In consequence of [DOT]that Bannister's feet were severely frozen and he felt so disgusted and indignant with his treatment that he sent in his resignation and left the service. This is left out of the report entirely. They also leave out of the report the complaint of Bannister to the effect that he received no remuneration as choir master in the Protestant chapel while the guard who acted in the same capacity in the Roman Catholic

chapel received $50 a year for his services besides other perquisites. They attempt to summarize the evidence of Bryant by saying that his evidence and complaints were of no value. Bryant swore in his evidence *and this is left out entirely, that he had broken his wrist and was asked to go on duty alone in the ayslum with one hand ihelpless. He also swore that the deputy warden attempted to get him removed from office fourteen years ago on the ground of physical unfitness; but that man is still a guard in the institution. Another matter to which Bryant referred was that the deputy placed two insane convicts in the ward with Bryant alone one night about *midnight, locked the doors and left him there with these two men. About half an hour later the deputy sent a man to find out whether he had succeeded in placing those men in their cells or what had happened. These statements may seem very trivial, but I maintain that they indicate 'a lack of judgment on the part of the deputy warden which should not be passed over.
They say in the report, in referring to the evidence of Grier, at page 23:
The evidence of Grier is not corroborated by the prison records. The records show that Bishop attempted to hang himself on two occasions ; on July 9, 1S98, and March 22, 1899. On the former occasion he was cut down by Guard Davis; on the latter, by Guard Marsh. Grier does not appear in either case. There is no record of any other attempt at suicide by Bishop. If any occurred it should be in the record. Grier says he 'cut down' Bishop in 1906. The records show that Bishop died of tuberculosis in 1904.
I invite any hon. gentleman to refer to Grier's statement in the type-written evidence, it only occupies about one-half or two 'pages, and he will find that there is not a word to bear out the statement made by the commissioners in their report. Grier states most emphatically that he stopped to cut this man Bishop down when Bishop was attempting to commit suicide, and that he was late in winding his clock in consequence of stopping for this purpose. The deputy warden reprimanded him for being late in winding his clock. He told the reason he was late but the deputy warden said: Let him hang, you wind your clock, that is the first thing to do; let him hang, but wind pour clock. The report says that this statement stands alone. The statement does not stand alone. Marsh also swears to having a somewhat similar experience with the same convict. Marsh however, remembering the reprimand that Grier

had received from the deputy
11	p.m. did go and wind his clock first and then attended to the convict who was hanging himself and they had quite a time in bringing the convict to. What remark did the deputy make on that occasion? He exonerated Marsh and told him he did right, that the proper thing for him to do was to wind his clock first. At the time Grier was reprimanded by the deputy warden, in the way I have stated, he appealed to Hughes who was then head keeper and Hughes told him that in any case where he found the convict's life in danger the proper thing for him to do was to save that life. That statement is a corroboration of Grier's statement, and yet the commissisioners endeavoured in their report to represent this as never having occurred. There is absolutely nothing in Grier's evidence to support the statements that they made. Grier does not say what year it was he cut the convict down, he does not give the year at all; in fact he did not remember the year, but he did remember the occurrence and he remembered the statement the deputy warden had made in regard to that matter. They say this statement stands alone. I say it does not stand alone. I have already referred to what took place with regard to Aikin when he was late in winding his dock owing to his giving attention to a sick convict. On that occasion the deputy said:	Wind your clock, if he
dies you are not responsible. I mention these facts to show the minister and this House what I think it does clearly show, that this deputy warden is a man who is unfitted for the position he occupies. He has not that sense of humanity which a man should have who occupies that important position. They say there is nothing in the evidence to indicate any cruelty of disposition on the part of the deputy. I have cited the evidence of Grier, Marsh, Aikins and Bannister. Bannister said that he was refused the shanty which was ordinarily given to guards on duty in exposed places. I have cited the hosing of convicts which the commissioners say is cruel and inhuman and which the evidence shows clearly was performed by O'Leary himself on many occasions.
Then, there is the matter of tubbing. The commissioners say that this tubbing is inhuman. Six or eight swore to tubbing having been done. There is no doubt about it having been done. Did not the deputy warden know that that was going on? If he did not know that that was going on,
I ask this committee, is a man of that kind a fit and proper person to hold the responsible position he holds?
How is this tubbing carried on? There are apliances for inflicting this punishment. The convict's clothes are taken off, his feet are strapped together, his arms are strapped to his sides, and he is then immersed in a tub of water which may be ice cold or just moderately cold, depending on the season of the year. Many of them were tubbed in the months of January and February. These men, strapped as I have indicated, were shoved down under the water by the guards, and when they came up were shoved down again. As one guard testified, they were shoved down till the bubbles came to the surface. The evidence given before that commission proves conclusively that that was done in that institution, and I say that the deputy warden more than any other man was responsible for its being done. Bear in mind that the deputy warden placed the convicts in their positions and the guards in their positions, and if he did not know it was going on he should have known. Dr. Phelan knew, because he said he posted up a notice that it must not continue. Just imagine it. Many of the men who were treated in this manner were insane. Guard Bryant gave evidence before the commission in regard to tubbing-page 787. He says he saw convicts with legs strapped together and arms strapped to the sides put into the water:
Q. They (the guards) would lift them up and put them in the water?-A Yes.
Q. Would they go right down below the surface?-A. They would just go down and up again.
Q. Down below the surface?-A. Yes.
Q. Would their heads go under the water?- A. Yes, their heads would go in the water.
Q. And picked up?

A. Picked up at once by the guard.
Q. And go down and picked up again?-A Yes.
Q. Who would give that order?-A. By the authorities.
Q. Who would that be?-A. Either the warden, the deputy warden, or the doctor could give that order.
Q. Either one of the three?-A. Yes.
Take the evidence of another man, Wesley Babcock, who helped in the tubbing-page 796.
Q. Ever see a prisoner put in the tub to give him a cold bath?-A. Yes.
Q. Where was that?-A. Asylum.
Q. By whose orders?-A Mr. McWatters.
Q. What office did he hold?-A. Acting keeper, I think, at the time.
Q. Why was the tubbing done?-A He insulted another officer.

And this was an insane man!
Q. How did you proceed to punish this man? -A. Filled the tub with water and put him into it.
Q. And held him down?-A. Tes.
Q. In the cold water?-A. Tes.
Dr. Etherington. An insane patient!
By Mr. Downey :
Q. An insane patient who was guilty of insulting one of the officers, and who was subjected to this for punishment for the offence: that is right?-A. Tes.
Dr. Etherington: It is important to know whether insane patients are punished or not.
By Mr. Downey:
Q. How long did they keep him in the cold bath?-A. I could not tell you how long they kept him in. They kept him in till he gave up, till he said he was sorry for what he had done; that is all I know.
By Mr. Stewart:
Q. Was he held under the water?-A Tes.
Q. Was he there half an hour?-A. No, he would have been dead if he was.
Q. Was he pushed down in the water?-A He was.
Q. Was he smothering when he came up?-A. He was.
Q. Did you ever see blood coming out of the mouths and noses of convicts treated in that way?-A. Not out of him.
Q. Did you like that treatment?-A. I would not want it myself.
I could read similar testimony by other guards who took part in this tubbing, which went on to a considerable extent in this institution, and which was performed, as some of the guards stated, at the order of the deputy warden or the doctor. The doctor himself says that when he heard of it he issued an order against that sort of thing, and it is only fair to him to accept his statement. Now let us look at the evidence of Douglas Stewart in regard to hosing, given on pages 17 and 18:
Q. Tou And this (hosing) more efficient (than the triangle) ?-A. More effective.
Q. What is it that makes it so effective with these convicts?-A. It takes the defiance out of them.
Q. How?-A. If you got the hose you would know.
Q. What is it?

A. I suppose it is the impact of the hose against the body, knocks the wind out of them.
Q. And it seems to succeed where nothing else will?-A. Tes, it never failed yet.
Q. To beat an incorrigible convict into submission?-A. Tes.
And, further on:
Q. Is that the most severe punishment?-A. No, I think shooting is more severe.
y. You mean Killing a man outright?-A. Tes.
When Inspector Stewart was asked what pressure was on the hose, he said it would be 60 lbs. to the inch. The commissioners state that they saw the hose, not being

used on a convict, bnt in the hosing cell. They state that when the nozzle was put through the bars the water struck the opposite wall in an almost unbroken stream. A stream of water at that pressnre would strike a man a pretty severe blow. Stewart also stated in his evidence that the pressnre at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary was 75 lbs. to the inch. I suppose they need a little more force there to-make the convicts give in. I want to impress this fact upon the committee, that, although hosing is provided in the regulations, those regulations were drawn np by the inspectors, at least, that is my understanding. It is all right to say that Sir Oliver Mowat, when Minister of Justice, acceded to this. I can well understand the inspector, who had practical control of the penitentiaries, asking the assent of the Minister of Justice to certain regulations. It would not be a matter into which Sir Oliver Mowat would look very closely, but the inspector knew from having seen the hose used what effect it would have. My own opinion is that it is cruel and inhuman. Tubbing is not authorized by the regulations, as I understand them, but tubbing has been carried on in that institution, and even insane convicts have been subjected to that treatment. I say that it is a disgrace to the Dominion of Canada if we allow this thing to go on in the future.
Mr. BIOKERDIKlE : Hear, hear. It is a shame.

I have no maudlin sentiment for a convict who has violated the laws of society. He has to be punished, but he should not be treated as if he were a brute; he should be treated with soma humanity, and I say that the evidence taken by that commission shows that these convicts have not been treated like human beings; they have been treated like dogs or worse. Talk about reformation! How, in the name of Heaven, can you reform a man when all the time he is subjected to this kind of treatment! What must be his feelings? It is impossible to reform him under those conditions.
I make another charge against the deputy, and which indicates his absolute unfitness for the position he occupies. He admitted in his evidence that it was up to him to	appoint	the convicts to
their positions in the prison, and also the guards to their positions. I went through that institution in company with the present warden, Colonel Irvine.

We visited the various shops-the carpenter shop, the paint shop, the blacksmith shop- and, lastly, we came around to the stone pile, and saw sixty convicts sitting there breaking stone. They say there is nothing else for them to do, that there is no place else to put them. Perhaps some recognition must be given to that statement; but the deputy warden, if he had the instincts of humanity and the common sense of a five-year-old young one, would not place a boy convict of fourteen or fifteen years on that stone pile, and keep him there for three or four years cracking stone. If there was not another charge to level against the deputy warden, the one fact that he would take boys fourteen and fifteen years old, place them beside old repeaters, and keep them on that stone pile year after year, is sufficient to indicate that the man is not fit for the position he occupies. If you go through that institution and look at the faces of those convicts on that stone pile, you will see an expression that is almost impossible to conceive.
Is it not a fact that in some of our penitentiaries men are chained down with logging chains in the dark dungeons?
I think it is. It was brought out in the evidence that at Kingston they were sentenced to the dungeon and shackled to the gate.
I have more reference to St. Vincent de Paul.

I want to give you another instance of the absolute unfitness of this man, O'Leary, for the position which he occupies. Fancy, on that stone pile, sixty men breaking stone month after month and year after year, a pail of water, and all drinking out of one cup and from one pail. Not only that, but it was brought out in the evidence that men with syphilitic sores in their mouths were in the same gangs with these boys, and all drinking out of the same pail and out of the same cup. x submit that you would not put a diseased animal alongside of healthy ones, and yet you put men with the most loathsome disease you can imagine alongside these boys and expect them to grow up to strong and vigorous manhood.
Was that fact known to the officials of the institutions?
Certainly it was known to the officials; it was admitted in their evidence.

They should have
known of it.

Let me give you another instance of the way in which this institution has been run. This has been the routine treatment meted out to sick convicts. On Sundays, in order to let the guards go home, the sick convicts were given their breaklasv at nine o'clock, their dinner at eleven, ana their supper at one o'clock and they got nothing more to eat until between eight and nine o'clock on Monday morning. This was the way in which they treated sick convicts.
Supper at one o'clock?

That is what I said.
They got their meals at nine, eleven and one and the only part of their meal that they could keep in their cells was a piece of bread; they were not allowed to retain any of the dishes. There may have been a difference of opinion as to whether an investigation of this institution was necessary when I made my charges, but there can now be no two opinions in this country in regard to it being necessary.

I would like my hon.
friend to repeat that statement about sick convicts receiving their meals at the hours mentioned. Does he mean to say that they got their meals at nine, eleven and one o'clock, and nothing between that and next day?
That is what I say. They received their breakfast at nine, their dinner at eleven, and their supper at one, and nothing from that time until Monday morning between eight and nine o'clock.
On Sunday only?
On Sunday only.
Is the hon. gentleman referring to the evidence brought out?

I am referring to what is brought out and what appears in the typewritten evidence which I have here. I shall be very glad if any hon. member desires it, to corroborate any statement I make by the evidence, which bears out what I have said.
Why does the hon. gentleman lay so much blame on the deputy warden? Was not the warden responsible for all these Acts?

I will answer that question. Under our system, as it is now and has been for many years, the warden-ships in penitentiaries have gone as

political plums to men, no matter which side has been in power. There was no consideration given to the man's fitness for the position of warden. He got the position of warden because of services he had rendered to his party. As a result of that the warden depended upon the next officials, the deputy warden, the surgeon, and so on, for the administration of the penitentiary.

In the case of sick
convicts is not the diet fixed by the doctor?
Yes, by the doctor. I am not charging that particular point against the deputy warden; I am charging it against the doctor.
It is incredible that they should be left without anything to eat from one o'clock on Sunday until next day.

That is admitted in
the evidence. I am not stating anything I cannot prove. As a result of the warden-ship being a political appointment, the administration of this institution largely rests with the deputy warden. That is recognized, and the deputy warden places the guards in their various positions and assigns the convicts to their work. I hold him responsible. The point I am trying to make in regard to the deputy is that all these matters indicate, at least to my mind, that the deputy does not possess that tact and judgment which a man should possess in administering a large institution of that kind.
I understand that a convict is not allowed to have a newspaper and that he is not even allowed to have his mother's photograph in his cell. Is that correct?

I do not know about the photograph. I do not think he is allowed to have his mother's photograph, and generally convicts are not allowed to have newspapers, though I believe there are some convicts in that institution to-day who have certain privileges along that line which are not enjoyed by other convicts. They have been allowed to have not only newspapers, hut their pipes and tobacco. I know a convict in that institution who is looking for parole to-day. He is one of the men who came up before the -commission and whose evidence was made much of by the commission. I refer to Travers. Many hon. members in this House have heard of Mr. Travers. When
Mr. Travers was taken to Toronto he was in charge of one of the officials of the institution, and he was taken there to give evidence before Mr. Justice Meredith. The lines were relaxed to such an extent that Travers was enabled to go to a certain liquor store in Toronto and order	some	whisky to be sent toan	official in	the penitentiary.
Not only that, but he, by letter, ordered cigars and whisky from a man in eastern Ontario to have it sent to him at the penitentiary, and stated that he would pay for it some day. Whether it was sent or not I do not know, but I do know that the letter was sent. The letter got out and went to this man in eastern Ontario asking him to send the cigars.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that in the evidence given before the commission.
No, and there are other things not in the evidence given before the commission.

The regulation says:
A convict whose conduct is satisfactory may receive visits from members of his family once in three months and may write to members of his family once in two months. He may 'receive letters from relative or friends, but such letters must be short and devoted exclusively to family or business matters.' No enclosure such as newspaper clippings, pictures, cards, stamps, etc., are delivered. Christmas boxes, hampers or packages of fruit, food or confectionery are not permitted to be sent to the prison.

I want to pursue the
report of this kalsomining trio a little bit further. I notice that the chairman of the commission is a K.C., and we all know what that usually means, but in this case if yon turn the letters around you will have them to mean chief kalsominer. On page 21 of the report I read:
We are referred by counsel quite properly on this charge to the evidence of Major Hughes, pages 239-244 to the rosters prepared by the deputy, as 'the best evidence in support of this charge' also to the evidence of Dr. Platt.
What docs Mr. Stewart in his argument say? He says:
The best evidence in support of this charge is found in the evidence of Major Hughes commencing at page 239 and continuing to page 244 inclusive, also rosters prepared by the deputy warden. I would also refer to the return made by the Secretary of State, a copy of which may be found at page 546 and 547 also to the evidence of Dr. Platt page 556 and the evidence of W. S. Hughes commencing at page 1660.
Why did they mangle what Mr. Stewart, the counsel, said; why did they suppress

or make no mention of the return, of the Secretary of State? I asked certain questions in this House which were answered by the Secretary of State, and I have here the answers given by him. These documents were put in as evidence before the commission, and I think they are very important documents as [DOT] indicating iavour-itism on the part of the deputy warden. It seems to me the commission deliberately left this out of the question. They also, it seems to me, deliberately do not refer to the evidence of Mr. Hughes at page 1660 which is very important evidence, and the evidence of Dr. Platt, at page 556, which is also very material. Why do they hunt out paragraphs here and there to try to make it appear that the warden was equally responsible with the deputy for the placing of guards in positions, and suppress Dr. Platt's testimony where he swears that after the keepers were done away with the guards have their positions assigned to them by the deputy warden, and yet this report tries to make it appear that the warden is equally responsible for assigning the guards. The deputy warden himself admitted that the responsibility was his and that he alone was the man who assigned the guards to their positions. This was all verified when the deputy warden was on the stand, and when the report of the Secretary of State was placed before him and he was questioned. The names were taken one at a time and he was asked with regard to each one and he corroborated the report of the *Secretary of State. These men were appointed to these positions by him and that *report shows conclusively that there was *favouritism on the part of the deputy warden. I do not know whether it was done consciously or unconsciously but the deputy warden certainly favoured the guards and keepers of his own religion in [DOT]that institution. If you take the return presented by the Secretary of State you *will find that when there were keepers in the institution, out of eleven of them seven were Roman Catholics and four Protestants. If you look at that return you will find
that under disciplinary officers, eleven out of twenty were Roman Catholics and nine were Protestants. I say that consciously or unconsciously the deputy warden has favoured men of his own religion in that institution, and that that was one of the causes of lack of harmony which prevailed. These remarks are taken from the Conservative press. I turn to the Liberal press. Some little time ago the hon. member for
Frontenac made the rather drastic remark that the members of this commission, instead of being worth fifteen dollars a day, were not worth fifteen cents a day, and this appeared in the British Whig some days later:
The Whig is under no obligation to defend these men politically, as they owed their choice, primarily, to the fact that they were good Conservatives. But they possessed, apart from their political calling, special qualifications for the work. Mr. Macdonell, the chairman, had for many years given penology a very close study. He was largely interested in the reform of erring humanity. Dr. Etherington was chosen, it is presumed, because of his professional train- [DOT] ing, and because one very distinct phase of the inquiry was of a man of unbiased mind, Mr. Downey was, in a sense, a specialist in the service to which he was called in this ease.
The commission had its experiences during the inquiry.
Perhaps I should say in regard to Mr. Downey that I knew Mr. Downey slightly in the Ontario Legislature. Mr. Downey acted as chairman of the Prison Commission appointed by the Hon. W. J. Hanna, then provincial secretary for Ontario, and I have always understood he framed the Teport upon which the Ontario system was brought into existence. So much for the commission.
I want to say, as regards the hon. member for Frontenac, that I give him every credit for being honestly and zealously filled with a desire to reform conditions at the Kingston penitentiary. He enjoyed to a degree that I did not the confidence of now Inspector Hughes and several of the guards of that institution. They told their stories to him, as I understand it, and, believing that evidence was evidence upon which he could rely, he made certain specific charges to the minister, and, as a result of these charges, and, possibly, as a result of the attention drawn to penitentiary administration in general, the minister appointed a commission. But, at the beginning, an unfortunate thing happened, and I say unfortunate in this sense: that I think it militated somewhat against the general good work and reputation of the commissioners. When the commission was received in Kingston it was found that there was a five-year limit placed on the examination or scrutiny into the chargee that were made by Dr. Edwards. At the very inception of the inquiry that caused trouble. Perhaps I may make the remark that, during the entire inquiry, the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) put himself with all his energy behind the investigation that

he had instituted. No effort was1 too great, and no detail too small to have his consideration. He attended the sittings of the commission daily, from their beginning to their end, and did everything that was possible for a man to do to bring before the commission such evidence as he thought should have their hearing and consideration. But Dr. Edwards and the commissioner fell foul of one another at almost the first sitting of the commission. iA discussion took place at that first meeting, at which I happened to be, as to the construction that was to be put on the terms * of the commission. The commissioners ruled as follows:
The intention of the commission is to have an investigation of present conditions in the prison. The charges that were made refer to the present state and management of the penitentiary, and that, primarily, is the subject to be investigated. That goes without saying. The commission is not charged with investigating what was a past condition of things, five, or ten, or twenty years ago; we are to investigate the conditions of things today. In order to investigate the condition of things to-day, it may be necessary to go beyond the time limit of five years, and that the commission has power to do. The terms of the commission express that quite clearly, and I do not think it could be better expressed, that where, in any particular matter, the commission deems it in the public interest to pursue the inquiry beyond the five year limit, they are to do so.
The vexation and irritation arose out of this fact. Certain of Dr. Edwards' charges referred to a period anterior to five years of the date of the appointment of the commission, and one of these was a perjury charge. The charges made by Dr. Edwards against Deputy Warden O'Leary were:
I charge Deputy Warden O'Leary:
(a)	With petty and persistent persecution of guards and keepers;
(h) With political partisanship.
(c)	With testifying falsely at investigation held at the prison;

The charges made by Dr. Edwards against Dr. Phelan were:
I charge the surgeon, Dr. Phelan:
(a)	With gross political partisanship;
(b)	With, using violent and indecent language to a guard in the presence of others;

Yes.

Then how does the hon. gentleman square that with the statement of the chairman of the commission in these words:
The charges that were made refer to the present state, etc.

I do not think the hon. member is justified in taking that position at all. Any reasonable person will agree with me that the thing for me to discuss here would naturally be the charges which were made. I regret to say that I took rather too much time in discussing them, and stated very specifically that I regretted I could not express an opinion on the other matter. If the hon. member had done me the justice to consider what was written in the papers, he would find that I expressed myself very clearly at the outset of the investigation that my opinion was that it mattered very little who occupied the positions of officials in the penitentiary; that our object in holding the inquiry was the reforming of conditions.

I do not wish to quarrel with my hon. friend's method of expressing his ideas. I give to him the same privilege of thought to which I think I am entitled, in trying to come to a just and fair conclusion as to the value of the report of this commission.
I wantyto direct the attention of the House to one or two small discrepancies in the story of the hon. member for Frontenac, and to show what I mean by saying that a man can hold a cent so close to his eye that he can blind the sun. That is the charge he was drawing to the attention of the chairman. How I happened to know about this matter is this:	The

He explained to me that the chairman of the commission had been unfair in sending Johnston home and he also told me that, as he understood the matter, Jobnston had not placed his evidence before the chairman
of the commission. With my hon. friend's concurrence I wrote to the chairman of the commission, who replied to me that Johnston had told his story to him that day and that, after he had heard the story, he said to him:	You had better go home and say

Do you think the chairman of the commission was justified in doing that?
Mr. NI'CKLE:	I think he was justified
and for this reason-

The commission might as well be divided into three parts and each one take certain evidence. What was the benefit of having their combined judgment in regard to the matter, if one man was going to say what should be presented and what should be excluded?
Mr. NI'CKLE: It is a fallacy to argue in that way, for this reason. When complaint was made to the commission about the conduct of the chairman, as complained of by the hon. member for Frontenac, the commission that afternoon had Johnston called, and Johnston gave his evidence, and the then conclusion of the commission was that it was of such a trivial character that it had no weight and as well might never have been given before the commissioners.
